### SU-AUTH-004 — Logout is not yet demonstrably complete

File: [auth/logout/route.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/api/auth/logout/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L8-L45)

The logout route correctly delegates token revocation to the backend and attempts to clear cookies at the BFF layer.

However, its cookie-clearing code specifies `path: '/'` without explicitly specifying a domain. Cookie deletion must match the original cookie's name, domain and path scope.

It also discards backend `Set-Cookie` headers and reconstructs the clearing cookies itself.

Architectural risk: If the original cookies were issued with a different domain or path, some authentication cookies could survive logout.

Required verification: Inspect the shared authentication cookie issuer and test logout using the actual production cookie attributes. We should not assume that the current clearing logic is sufficient merely because it sets `maxAge: 0`.

### SU-AUTH-005 — Test fixture session endpoint requires deployment-level protection

File: [test-fixture-session/route.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/api/auth/test-fixture-session/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L16-L40)

This endpoint can mint a short-lived learner token. Its existing safeguards include environment checks, a long shared secret, constant-time comparison, an allowlist of fixture IDs and a 15-minute token lifetime.

These are meaningful protections.

The remaining architectural question is whether the `PROJECT_LLM_ISOLATED_VERIFICATION` override can ever be enabled in a production-equivalent deployment outside the intended isolated environment.

Assessment: Not a confirmed vulnerability. It is a privileged testing capability that needs explicit deployment isolation and negative security tests.

## New finding SU-TEST-002 — Proxy tests appear inconsistent with the implementation

P1 — Test reliability

File: [src/\_\_tests\_\_/proxy.test.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/__tests__/proxy.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L12-L50)

This test imports both `proxy` and `isPublicAuthRoute` from `../proxy`.

However, the reviewed [src/proxy.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/proxy.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) exports `proxy` and `config`, not `isPublicAuthRoute`.

Additionally, the test expects an unauthenticated dashboard request with `?_rsc=test` to bypass authentication. That expectation needs to be reconciled with the proxy's stated security requirement to protect React Server Component requests.

Assessment: The test source is inconsistent with the inspected implementation. This is a concrete test-suite defect candidate, not proof of a production authentication bypass.

Verification: Execute the Vitest suite and check the current intended RSC authorization contract before updating either the test or implementation.

## New finding SU-TEST-003 — Progress tests verify routing, but not privacy

File: [tutorial/progress/route.test.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/api/tutorial/progress/route.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L9-L32)

These tests verify upstream URL normalization, internal-key forwarding and unauthenticated request rejection.

They do not assert that successful progress responses carry `Cache-Control: private, no-store`, nor do they test malformed payloads, cross-brand access or upstream failure behavior.

Assessment: Existing tests are useful but insufficient to close the earlier progress API findings.

## Updated architectural conclusions

The source inspected in this tranche supports three important decisions:

1. Preserve the shared authentication architecture. Login and refresh routes already delegate to a shared authority; duplicating authentication logic inside SkillUp would be counterproductive.
2. Resolve identity, logout and caching contracts together. These concerns cross the BFF, shared authentication package, browser state and service worker. Reviewing them independently would miss important interactions.
3. Treat test quality as part of architecture quality. A test suite that asserts outdated behavior cannot serve as a trustworthy acceptance gate.

The next major code-review area is the SkillUp learner data layer, particularly `skillup-data.ts`, its API callers and the authoritative backend implementations. That is where we must verify that learner profiles, attendance, payments, enrollment and progress respect the `skillup_prod` ownership rules.

Review status: The complete application inventory is established, but the full 137-file review and shared-dependency review are not complete. All findings remain subject to the stated verification requirements. No code, commits or pull requests have been created or modified.

# SkillUp Principal Architect Audit — Learner Data Layer

This tranche covers the five remaining files in `apps/skillup-web/src/lib/`, including the complete 624-line `skillup-data.ts`.

The most consequential finding is that the learner data module directly accesses multiple domain databases and constructs several user-facing values that may not reflect actual records.

That is a stronger architectural concern than file size alone.

## Finding SU-DATA-001 — Cross-domain database coupling

P1 — Architecture boundary

[skillup-data.ts, lines 1–35](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/lib/skillup-data.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L1-L35)

The module imports Drizzle, PostgreSQL Pool, `@quiz/db-people` and `@quiz/db-placement`. It also creates a direct payment database connection.

The current dependency pattern is:

SkillUp application data module

People DB

Placement DB

Payment DB

Direct read access is not automatically a data-ownership violation. However, this module combines persistence, business calculations, presentation mapping and fallback policy.

Architectural decision required: Identify the authoritative services for people, enrollment, payments and placement. SkillUp should consume governed contracts rather than independently reimplementing each domain's rules.

## Finding SU-DATA-002 — Fallback data can misrepresent learner state

P1 — Data correctness

[skillup-data.ts, fallback learner records](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/lib/skillup-data.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L88-L122)

The file defines example batch, session and placement data. When a learner has no active batch, `getSkillupMyBatch()` returns the example batch rather than an explicit no-enrollment state (lines 312–318).

For placement, the code also returns a fallback profile when no actual placement profile exists (lines 448–457).

This means a learner could see an apparently real batch or placement profile that does not belong to their actual records.

Recommendation for the eventual implementation: Return an explicit empty or not-enrolled state for authenticated learner data. Keep demonstration fixtures isolated from production data contracts.

## Finding SU-DATA-003 — Dashboard metrics may not represent their labels

[skillup-data.ts, dashboard aggregation](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/lib/skillup-data.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L248-L310)

The dashboard calculates attendance percentage using all batch sessions as the denominator, while the numerator counts the learner's present attendance records. It also selects the first session as a fallback when no scheduled session exists.

The placement match count is simply the number of open job listings, not the number of learner-specific matches.

Assessment: These are confirmed calculation and naming patterns. The correct business formulas need to be established with the domain owners before changing them.

## Finding SU-DATA-004 — Payment data has two inconsistent access paths

[Dashboard payment query](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/lib/skillup-data.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L248-L263) and [Payments page query](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/lib/skillup-data.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L374-L417)

The dashboard obtains payment installments through `@quiz/db-people`, while the dedicated payments function queries a separate payment database through `pg`.

This creates two independent paths for related financial information, with different query logic and potentially different underlying records.

Priority: P1 — data consistency. We need to establish the authoritative payment service and verify that both screens derive amounts, statuses and balances from the same governed source.

## Finding SU-DATA-005 — Synthetic placement match scores

[Placement ranking and fallback logic](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/lib/skillup-data.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L448-L509)

When there is no placement profile, the code generates match scores from list positions. When vector matching fails, it generates scores using the learner's readiness score and list positions.

Those numbers are not necessarily calculated job-to-learner matches.

Priority: P1 — learner-facing correctness. The application should distinguish verified matching results from unavailable recommendations rather than present fabricated percentages as measured results.

## Finding SU-API-002 — Inconsistent authentication helpers across API routes

The nine API routes reviewed in this tranche show two patterns:

- Student dashboard, attendance, payments, placement, batches and my-batch routes use `requireStudentAuth`.
- Programs and faculty routes use `extractAuthFromRequest` followed by `enforceBrandValidation`.

Both patterns authenticate, but their exact token, role and identity requirements may differ. That needs a shared contract review, particularly because the same brand's endpoints should not disagree about which identities are valid.

## Finding SU-API-003 — Personalized API responses lack explicit no-store headers

The six reviewed learner-specific routes return `NextResponse.json(...)` without explicit `Cache-Control: private, no-store`.

That is not proof that an intermediary is caching their responses, but it is inconsistent with the stricter cache policy already used by the tutorial sections endpoint.

Priority: P1 — privacy defense in depth, especially in combination with the service-worker concern.

## Finding SU-DATA-006 — Error and fallback behavior needs separation

The public catalog and faculty data helpers silently return example data on database errors. This can make an unavailable database look like a functioning catalog.

The correct contract should distinguish a real empty result, temporary service unavailability and explicitly configured demonstration data.

## Additional file assessments

The smaller modules are more cohesive:

| File                          | Assessment                                                                                                                                 |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `skillup-types.ts`            | Clear presentation data types; no major architectural violation found in this file                                                         |
| `skillup-format.ts`           | Small, cohesive formatting utilities; date/time-zone behavior needs tests                                                                  |
| `certificate-verification.ts` | Appropriate certificate lookup responsibility; upstream response is cast rather than runtime-validated                                     |
| `skillup-api.ts`              | Centralizes server-side API fetching but also forwards identity headers and implements selective fallbacks; trust-boundary review required |

Important review boundary: The findings above are grounded in source code, but I have not yet inspected every database schema, service owner or deployment configuration necessary to finalize remediation designs.

The next dependency review must establish the exact relationship among `@quiz/db-people`, `@quiz/db-placement`, the payment database and the canonical SkillUp learner identity. That will determine which changes belong in SkillUp and which belong in shared backend services.

Status: Read-only audit continues. No source changes, commits, pull requests or executed test results are being claimed.

# SkillUp Principal Architect Audit — Database Ownership and Domain Contracts

I have continued into the shared packages that SkillUp depends on, using the same authoritative feature branch. This tranche reviews the actual database schemas and placement matching implementation, not just the learner-facing application.

The key result: The earlier payment inconsistency is now confirmed at the schema level. The identity contract also needs a formal decision before we can safely design changes.

## 1. SU-DATA-004 — Two separate payment-installment models

P1 — Confirmed schema divergence

People database

[payment-installments.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-people/src/schema/payment-installments.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

- `studentUserId`
- `label`
- `dueDate`
- `amount`
- `status`
- `paymentRef`

Payment database

[payment-installments.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-payment/src/schema/payment-installments.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

- `planId`
- `installmentNumber`
- `dueDate`
- `amount`
- `status`
- `paymentRef`

The Payment database has a separate `payment_plans` table with its own user reference and plan status.

These are not identical representations of one table. The SkillUp dashboard reads the People representation, while the payments page reads the Payment representation.

Architectural assessment: There is a confirmed duplication of financial data concepts. We have not yet established whether one is a legacy model, a read projection or an independently maintained record.

Before implementation, we must trace the write paths and synchronization mechanism. The target architecture should designate a single financial authority and make any secondary representation explicitly derived.

## 2. SU-IDENTITY-002 — User identity crosses incompatible domain types

The schemas show three distinct identity representations:

| Domain                                 | User reference  | Type                                |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| People `users`                         | `id`            | UUID primary key                    |
| People `batch_enrollments`             | `studentUserId` | UUID foreign key to People users    |
| Payment `payment_plans`                | `userId`        | UUID without a database foreign key |
| Placement `student_placement_profiles` | `userId`        | Text                                |

Sources: [People user schema](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-people/src/schema/users.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [Payment plan schema](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-payment/src/schema/payment-plans.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and [Placement profile schema](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-placement/src/schema/student-placement-profiles.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

A UUID represented as text is not inherently wrong. The architectural risk is which identity the value represents.

Earlier, `requireStudentAuth()` was found to prefer `shadowUserId`. The learner data module then passes that value into People, Payment and Placement queries.

We must verify that all three domains expect the SkillUp-local shadow identity. If one expects the original global identity instead, a valid learner could receive missing or incorrect records.

Priority: P1 — cross-domain identity contract.

## 3. SU-PLACEMENT-001 — Vector matching and display percentages have different semantics

The [placement vector service](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-placement/src/vector.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L144-L153) performs a real similarity query against Upstash Vector.

That is a positive implementation finding.

However, the learner data module converts the returned similarity score into a displayed percentage. On matching failure, it generates replacement percentages from readiness scores and list positions.

A vector similarity score is not automatically a calibrated probability of job suitability.

Architectural requirement: Define what “match percentage” means, document its calculation and distinguish measured similarity from fallback ordering.

## 4. SU-DB-001 — Shared database connection management

The [People DB client](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-people/src/db.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and [Payment DB client](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-payment/src/db.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) both provide lazy connection initialization, connection pooling and configured timeouts.

These are positive reliability measures.

But `skillup-data.ts` creates an additional payment `pg.Pool` independently of the shared payment package. That bypasses the common connection-management implementation.

Priority: P2 — consistency and operational governance.

## 5. SU-DATA-007 — Session and attendance metrics need stronger domain definitions

The reviewed schemas and application logic raise additional questions about how attendance and learner progress are calculated.

For example, the dashboard counts present attendance records but divides by the number of batch sessions. It does not visibly constrain that attendance query to the currently selected batch.

This can produce incorrect results if a learner has attendance records from other batches or if future sessions are included in the denominator.

Priority: P1 — business correctness.

## Architectural checkpoint

The evidence now supports prioritizing these areas for eventual remediation:

1. Establish one canonical identity-mapping contract across People, SkillUp, Payment and Placement.
2. Establish the authoritative payment ledger and eliminate ambiguous financial read paths.
3. Remove misleading production fallback learner data.
4. Correct learner-specific attendance and progress calculations.
5. Standardize authenticated response caching and session lifecycle behavior.

These are audit priorities, not approved implementation changes.

The baseline is still incomplete. Remaining work includes the shared authentication implementation, domain write paths, tutorial/quiz services, page components, configuration, deployment controls and test execution.

I will continue with those dependencies under the same Principal Architect framework. No code has been modified.

# SkillUp Principal Architect Audit — Shared Authentication and Identity Contracts

This review tranche exposes a confirmed contradiction between the shared identity rules and the identity passed into SkillUp database queries.

The contradiction is in source code, not merely a difference in naming.

## SU-IDENTITY-003 — Conflicting definitions of the database user ID

P1 — Cross-domain correctness risk

The shared [identityGuard.ts, lines 34–68](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/src/share-branding/auth/identityGuard.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L34-L68) explicitly requires `originalUserId` for database operations.

It states that `shadowUserId` is for cross-brand tracking and must not be used for database queries.

The [unifiedBffAuth.ts, lines 199–209](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/src/share-branding/auth/unifiedBffAuth.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L199-L209) header builder follows that contract by assigning `originalUserId` to `x-user-id`.

But the same module returns `shadowUserId` in its generic `auth.userId` field (line 152). The SkillUp learner routes pass `auth.userId` from their own authentication helper into database queries.

Verified JWT identity claims

originalUserId

Required for DB access by identityGuard

shadowUserId

Used as generic auth.userId by unifiedBffAuth

SkillUp learner database queries

Which identity is authoritative?

Principal Architect assessment: The contract inconsistency is confirmed. Incorrect data retrieval is a plausible consequence, but it has not been demonstrated against real records.

The required solution is not a blind replacement of one ID with another. We must trace the token issuer, People user mapping, enrollment creation and placement/payment record creation to establish the correct identifier for each domain.

## SU-AUTH-006 — Logout cookie mismatch is now confirmed in source

P1 — Session lifecycle

The shared cookie middleware issues SkillUp authentication cookies with a configured domain, defaulting to `.skillupitacademy.com`.

Source: [cookie.middleware.ts, lines 93–112](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/middleware/cookie.middleware.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L93-L112).

The shared middleware also provides `clearAuthCookies()`, which clears those cookies using the same domain.

Source: [cookie.middleware.ts, lines 209–235](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/middleware/cookie.middleware.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L209-L235).

But SkillUp's logout BFF manually clears `accessToken`, `refreshToken` and `csrfToken` without a domain attribute.

Source: [logout/route.ts, lines 29–42](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/api/auth/logout/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L29-L42).

Confirmed: Cookie issuance and BFF deletion use different domain attributes. The BFF's deletion cookies therefore cannot be relied upon to remove the domain-scoped authentication cookies.

The backend may also clear cookies correctly; that must be checked before concluding that logout fails end to end.

The eventual remediation should reuse the shared cookie lifecycle contract rather than introducing another independent cookie-clearing implementation.

## SU-BRAND-001 — Brand validation rejects known mismatches but overlooks malformed headers

[brand-validator.middleware.ts, lines 37–45](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/middleware/brand-validator.middleware.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L37-L45)

The middleware converts a supplied `x-brand` or `x-platform` header into a supported brand only when its value is recognized.

If the header is present but unsupported, it becomes `undefined` and does not trigger the later header-versus-token mismatch check.

Assessment: This is a confirmed validation gap, not proof of unauthorized access. The signed token and hostname still undergo brand validation.

Priority: P2 — input-validation consistency.

## SU-BRAND-002 — Authentication wrapper relies on externally supplied auth context

[withBrandValidation(), lines 176–210](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/middleware/brand-validator.middleware.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L176-L210)

The generic `withBrandValidation()` wrapper reads `req.auth` or its context argument rather than independently verifying a token.

That is safe only when callers guarantee the supplied authentication context is already trusted.

Required verification: Inventory every caller and confirm that authentication precedes brand validation. The wrapper's use of `any` also weakens compile-time enforcement.

## SU-TEST-004 — Shared security tests cover spoofed domains

Two additional test files have been reviewed:

- [Cookie domain security tests](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/middleware/__tests__/cookie.middleware.security.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
- [Brand validation tests](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/middleware/__tests__/brand-validator.middleware.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

They contain meaningful cases for malicious lookalike domains, brand mismatches, localhost development hosts and invalid token-brand claims.

Positive finding: Domain spoofing is explicitly considered in the shared test suite.

Coverage gap: The reviewed tests do not establish that SkillUp logout removes cookies across all relevant scopes or that malformed brand headers are rejected.

### Principal Architect checkpoint

The shared [IDENTITY_GUIDE.md](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/src/share-branding/auth/IDENTITY_GUIDE.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com) reinforces the intended separation between original and shadow identities. That makes the inconsistency in `unifiedBffAuth.ts` especially important.

The identity guide's description of database ownership also needs reconciliation with the current database schemas and the governing architecture document. Documentation is useful evidence of intent, but it cannot override the actual approved domain ownership model.

Audit status: This tranche covers shared authentication extraction, identity guards, cookie lifecycle, brand validation, documentation and associated tests. The full application and dependency review is still open. No code has been modified, and no tests have been represented as executed.

# SkillUp Principal Architect Audit — Authentication Lifecycle and Gateway

I continued the read-only review into the shared authentication gateway, browser session lifecycle and server-side authentication middleware.

This tranche adds two particularly important findings: a session-validation option that does not currently validate sessions, and an authentication gateway fallback that needs failure-mode testing.

## SU-AUTH-007 — `requireValidSession()` does not validate a session

P1 — Security contract

Source: [auth.middleware.ts, lines 45–103](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/middleware/auth.middleware.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L45-L103)

The `authenticate()` method verifies the JWT. But when `options.requireSession` is true, lines 72–79 contain only a TODO and commented-out session validation.

The public `requireValidSession()` method then calls `authenticate()` with that option enabled.

Confirmed behavior: The method checks the access token, but does not consult the session repository to verify whether the session is revoked or expired.

This does not establish that every application route is vulnerable. Other layers may enforce revocation. We must inspect callers before determining exposure.

Required architecture: A method named `requireValidSession` must either enforce the complete session contract or be removed from security-sensitive use until it does.

## SU-AUTH-008 — JWT-derived role and brand defaults are unsafe as a general authentication pattern

Source: [auth.middleware.ts, lines 60–69](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/middleware/auth.middleware.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L60-L69)

The middleware constructs its authorization user with:

```
role: (payload.role || 'student') as Role,
brand: (payload.brand || 'realtutorialhub') as Brand
```

The fallback values and TypeScript assertions do not validate the runtime claims.

If a validly signed token lacks these claims, the middleware supplies defaults instead of rejecting it.

Assessment: Confirmed fail-open claim interpretation within this middleware. Exploitability depends on the token issuer, verifier and which routes use this class.

Priority: P1. The shared contract should require explicit, valid brand and role claims for protected operations.

## SU-GATEWAY-001 — Authentication fallback requires request-replay verification

Source: [authBffRoute.ts, lines 382–565](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/src/share-branding/auth/authBffRoute.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L382-L565)

The authentication proxy sends requests to the gateway first. If the gateway returns a server error or throws, it can retry against a fallback API when configured to allow fallback.

This is a deliberate resilience mechanism.

However, login, signup and refresh are state-changing operations. Retrying them after an uncertain upstream failure may duplicate an operation unless the backend provides idempotency guarantees.

Required verification: Inspect gateway configuration, fallback deployment settings and backend transaction/idempotency handling. A gateway timeout must not cause duplicate accounts or inconsistent token rotation.

## SU-AUTH-009 — Server authentication fetch trusts forwarded host context

Source: [serverAuthState.ts, lines 25–40](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/src/share-branding/auth/serverAuthState.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L25-L40)

The server constructs its profile API base URL using `x-forwarded-proto`, `x-forwarded-host` or `host`, then forwards the request cookies to that URL.

This may be appropriate behind a correctly configured trusted gateway. But it makes proxy-header provenance a security-critical deployment assumption.

Risk: If untrusted clients can influence the forwarded host, an authenticated server-side request could be directed to an unintended destination.

Assessment: Potential security issue, not a confirmed exploit. We need the gateway's header sanitization and host allowlist configuration before assigning a final severity.

## SU-AUTH-010 — Authentication failure and temporary unavailability are not consistently distinguished

In `serverAuthState.ts`, the implementation retries transient failures and avoids treating an initial 5xx response as an invalid session. That is positive.

However, after retries are exhausted, it returns `null`, the same value returned for an unauthenticated user.

A caller that interprets `null` as an instruction to log out could still conflate service unavailability with an expired session.

Priority: P2 — session resilience. The server authentication state contract should distinguish unauthenticated, authenticated and temporarily unavailable outcomes.

## SU-AUTH-011 — Refresh scheduling is time-based rather than token-aware

Source: [useAutoRefresh.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/src/share-branding/auth/useAutoRefresh.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L20-L126)

The hook refreshes every ten minutes and normally performs an initial refresh after 30 seconds. It correctly avoids immediate logout on network errors and 5xx responses.

The remaining concern is that the schedule is not tied to the actual access-token expiry. Browser sleep, inactive tabs and refresh-token rotation can introduce timing differences.

Priority: P2 — reliability. Validate the existing behavior under suspended tabs, multiple tabs and concurrent refresh requests before redesigning it.

| P1       | Production learner fallback data and synthetic match percentages | Confirmed behavior                                |
| P1       | Logout cookie-domain mismatch                                    | Confirmed BFF mismatch; end-to-end impact pending |
| P1       | Service-worker caching of potentially personalized content       | Potential exposure; browser test pending          |
| P1       | `requireValidSession()` does not check session state             | Confirmed implementation gap                      |
| P1       | Authorization claims receive default role and brand              | Confirmed implementation gap                      |
| P2       | Gateway fallback request replay                                  | Idempotency verification pending                  |
| P2       | Forwarded-host trust in server auth fetching                     | Deployment verification pending                   |
| P2       | Token-refresh timing and concurrency                             | Integration testing pending                       |

Principal Architect conclusion: The next review needs to trace these shared authentication mechanisms into their real backend callers, token issuance and gateway configuration. That is necessary to separate demonstrable production defects from architectural risks that are already mitigated elsewhere.

The audit remains evidence-first and read-only. I have not modified files, run tests or approved implementation changes. The complete repository-wide, line-by-line audit is not yet finished.

# SkillUp Principal Architect Audit — Backend Authentication and Session Revocation

This tranche follows the authentication flow beyond the SkillUp BFF into the API server and gateway. It adds several concrete findings and clarifies an earlier concern.

## SU-AUTH-012 — Backend logout clears cookies even when revocation fails

Source: [API server logout route](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/app/api/auth/logout/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L44-L129)

The backend attempts to revoke refresh tokens, catches failures, and then continues clearing authentication cookies using the shared `clearAuthCookies()` helper.

This is a positive defense against leaving a browser signed in when backend revocation encounters an error.

However, it also returns a successful logout response after a revocation exception. That means the browser may be signed out while a server-side session remains active.

Assessment: Confirmed error-handling behavior. Actual token reuse depends on the revocation and verification services.

This also refines the earlier cookie finding: the backend does issue domain-aware clearing cookies, but the SkillUp BFF currently strips those headers and replaces them with host-only deletion cookies. The BFF is therefore the critical point requiring correction and browser verification.

## SU-AUTH-013 — Session-management endpoints fabricate identity equivalence

P1 — Identity contract

Source: [sessions/route.ts, lines 33–60](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/app/api/auth/sessions/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L33-L60).

The backend builds an RBAC identity object with all three fields set to `payload.userId`:

```
userId: payload.userId,
originalUserId: payload.userId,
shadowUserId: payload.userId,
```

The single-session revocation route repeats the same pattern.

That directly contradicts the shared identity guide's requirement to preserve distinct original and shadow identities.

Confirmed: The routes construct a synthetic identity context rather than using independently verified identity claims.

Not yet confirmed: Whether this leads to a privilege escalation. The subsequent RBAC and session-service checks still need end-to-end verification.

## SU-BRAND-003 — Session routes use hostname substring matching

Source: [Session deletion brand selection](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/app/api/auth/sessions/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L114-L140).

The DELETE session route derives brand using `requestHostname.includes('skillup')` and `includes('skillhubcore')`. The individual-session revocation route also uses `includes('skillup')`.

This conflicts with the canonical hostname resolver and the shared tests that explicitly reject lookalike hostnames.

Priority: P1 — inconsistent trust boundary. Although a later brand-validation check exists, brand derivation should not use substring matching in security-sensitive routes.

## SU-SESSION-001 — Confirmed cross-user session revocation defect

P0 — Authorization boundary

This is the most significant new finding in the current tranche.

The API route authenticates the requester and obtains their user ID, then calls:

```
globalLogoutService.revokeSession(userId, sessionId, ip, brand)
```

Source: [Single-session DELETE route](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/app/api/auth/sessions/%5BsessionId%5D/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L86-L89).

The service then calls:

```
await brandTokenRepo.revokeById(sessionId);
```

Source: [GlobalLogoutService.revokeSession()](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/global-logout.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L104-L124).

Finally, the repository accepts an optional `userId`:

```
async revokeById(id: string, userId?: string) {
  const conditions = [eq(this.refreshTokensTable.id, id)];
  if (userId) {
    conditions.push(eq(this.refreshTokensTable.userId, userId));
  }
  // Update matching record
}
```

Source: [TokenRepository.revokeById()](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/repositories/token.repository.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L58-L70).

Confirmed defect: The service omits the available user-scoping argument. Consequently, the repository update is constrained by session ID but not by session owner.

An authenticated user who knows another user's session ID could potentially revoke that session within the selected database context.

The route's RBAC permission check does not establish ownership of the target session.

Recommended eventual correction: Make `userId` mandatory at the repository boundary, enforce ownership in the database update, and verify the affected row count. Add negative tests proving that one learner cannot revoke another learner's session.

This is a P0 security remediation candidate, although exploitability and production impact still require controlled verification. No exploit test has been performed.

## SU-SESSION-002 — Current-device detection can be misleading

Source: [getActiveSessions()](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/global-logout.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L70-L95).

When a device ID is absent, the service marks the first returned session as the current one.

But the repository orders sessions by `lastUsedAt` without specifying descending order:

[getUserSessions()](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/repositories/token.repository.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L143-L154).

The first result may therefore be the least recently used session rather than the current one.

Priority: P2 — session-management correctness. Current-session identification should be based on verified session identity, not an inferred list position.

## SU-BRAND-004 — Backend hostname resolution trusts several header sources

Source: [request-brand.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/lib/request-brand.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L54-L77).

The resolver considers `x-original-host`, `origin`, `x-forwarded-host`, `host` and a fallback hostname, in that order.

That is a flexible proxy compatibility mechanism, but the resulting value is trustworthy only if the gateway strips or replaces untrusted client-supplied forwarding headers.

Assessment: Deployment trust-boundary verification required. Do not assume a forged hostname can reach this code unchanged.

### Principal Architect decision

The session-revocation finding should be treated as an urgent security review item before release. It is sufficiently grounded in the source to justify prioritization without waiting for the entire audit to finish.

However, I am preserving your governance requirement: no implementation, commit, pull request or deployment change without explicit approval.

The remaining audit will continue into token issuance, refresh rotation, gateway routing, learner APIs and the rest of the repository. This is a substantial repository-wide re# Principal Architect Audit — Session Ownership and Gateway Trust

I continued tracing the confirmed session-revocation issue into the database-selection layer and the gateway's tenant-resolution logic.

The new evidence strengthens the session ownership finding, while also showing that the gateway already contains a useful security safeguard.

## 1. SU-SESSION-001 — Ownership enforcement is missing at the database mutation

P0 candidate — Security

The complete call chain now establishes that:

1. The session DELETE route authenticates the requester and obtains `userId`.
2. `GlobalLogoutService.revokeSession()` receives that `userId`.
3. The service calls `revokeById(sessionId)` without passing `userId`.
4. `TokenRepository.revokeById()` applies an ownership condition only if a user ID was supplied.

The brand database selector limits the operation to the selected brand's token database, but it does not compensate for the missing session-owner condition.

Sources: [Session service](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/global-logout.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L104-L125), [Token repository](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/repositories/token.repository.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L58-L70) and [Brand database selection](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/brand-db.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L93-L107).

This is a confirmed authorization defect in the source. It should be prioritized for security remediation before release, subject to controlled verification.

## 2. SU-GATEWAY-002 — Gateway brand resolution has a proper trust check

Positive security control

[Gateway internal-request validation](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/services/api-gateway/src/lib/request-brand.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L79-L103)

The gateway does not automatically trust `x-original-host` or `x-forwarded-host`.

It first requires a matching internal secret. Without that secret, it resolves the brand from the gateway's actual request hostname.

This is a meaningful safeguard against arbitrary client-supplied brand headers.

The remaining question is whether all routes use this resolver consistently and whether internal secrets are managed and rotated appropriately.

## 3. SU-AUTH-014 — Login confirms the original/shadow identity distinction

[LoginService, lines 174–234](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/login.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L174-L234)

The login service explicitly issues tokens containing:

- `userId`: the brand database user's ID.
- `originalUserId`: that same original ID.
- `shadowUserId`: the identity returned by the cross-platform identity bridge.

Refresh sessions are stored under the original user ID.

This establishes an important fact: the original and shadow identifiers are intentionally different concepts, even when their values happen to coincide for a particular user.

It strengthens the earlier finding that SkillUp learner queries must use an explicitly defined identity type rather than an ambiguously named `auth.userId`.

## 4. SU-AUTH-015 — Token refresh can lose the original login roles

P1 — Session correctness

[TokenRefreshService, lines 116–158](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/token-refresh.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L116-L158)

The login service passes roles and email into the access-token generator, but its refresh-token generation call does not visibly include those claims.

The refresh service later attempts to obtain `email` and `roles` from the old refresh-token payload. If they are absent, it defaults to an empty email and empty roles.

That creates a possible login-versus-refresh identity inconsistency.

What is confirmed: The two service call sites have different claim inputs, and refresh provides empty fallbacks.

What remains to verify: Whether the shared `TokenService` automatically enriches refresh tokens with those claims. Until that implementation is reviewed, this is a high-priority risk rather than a confirmed loss of roles.

## 5. SU-AUTH-016 — Token rotation is transactional, but concurrency needs testing

[Token rotation transaction](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/token-refresh.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L162-L189)

The service revokes the old refresh token and creates the replacement inside one database transaction. This is a positive design choice.

However, the code first reads the old token and later performs a revocation update that does not itself require `revoked = false`.

Two concurrent refresh requests could both read the same valid old session before either transaction completes. Whether both can issue usable replacements depends on database constraints and transaction behavior.

Priority: P1 — concurrency verification. A controlled parallel-refresh test is required before concluding that refresh-token replay is prevented.

## 6. SU-GATEWAY-003 — Gateway has a broad public route that needs explicit endpoint authorization

[SkillUp gateway routes](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/services/api-gateway/src/routes/routing-table.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L16-L26)

The gateway declares the SkillUp root route as `public: true`, while `/tutorial-v2` is explicitly authenticated.

This is not automatically a vulnerability: the SkillUp application's own middleware and API handlers may enforce authentication.

But the gateway cannot be assumed to protect every learner endpoint. The security review must verify that each downstream protected endpoint authenticates independently.

Priority: P1 — authorization coverage verification.

## 7. SU-GATEWAY-004 — Gateway proxy errors expose internal exception messages

[Gateway proxy error handler](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/services/api-gateway/src/index.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L253-L265)

When proxying throws, the gateway includes `error.message` in its HTTP 500 response.

Internal exception messages can contain upstream addresses or implementation details. The gateway already uses a safer generic response in its top-level error handler.

Priority: P2 — information disclosure. Apply the same generic-client-error policy to proxy failures, retaining detailed diagnostics only in server logs.

# Principal Architect Audit — Token Service and Refresh Security

The shared token implementation resolves one of the most important open questions from the previous tranche.

## SU-AUTH-015 — Refresh-token role loss is confirmed

P1 — Confirmed defect

The shared [TokenService.generateRefreshToken()](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/token.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L306-L331) signs a refresh token containing identity, audience, token type and brand claims. It does not include `email` or `roles`.

Later, [TokenRefreshService](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/token-refresh.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L126-L145) attempts to read those claims from that refresh token and substitutes empty values when they are absent.

The result is a concrete inconsistency:

After login

Roles populated

Access token receives roles from the user repository

After refresh

Roles become `[]`

Refresh token has no roles to restore

This can cause users to lose role-dependent access after their first token refresh.

Required correction: Refresh should reconstruct authorization claims from a trusted current source, with explicit policy for role changes and account revocation. Simply copying stale role claims into refresh tokens would not fully solve authorization freshness.

## 2. SU-AUTH-017 — JWT signing secrets have hardcoded fallback values

P1 — Configuration security

[TokenService secret initialization](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/token.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L78-L93)

When the JWT environment variables are absent, the shared service falls back to fixed test secrets.

This is a confirmed configuration behavior. It is not evidence that production currently uses those secrets.

The required control is to fail startup in non-test environments when required signing secrets are missing or insufficiently strong.

## 3. SU-AUTH-018 — Identity claims can be silently fabricated during token issuance

[Access-token generation](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/token.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L281-L303)

`generateAccessToken()` substitutes `payload.userId` when either `originalUserId` or `shadowUserId` is missing.

The verification methods subsequently require both claims to exist, but they cannot distinguish an independently resolved identity from one created by that fallback.

This weakens the identity contract established by the identity bridge.

Priority: P1. Production token issuance should require independently validated identity mappings, with explicit exceptions only for approved migration or testing workflows.

## 4. SU-AUTH-019 — Gateway permits a signed token without a brand claim

P1 — Brand isolation

[Gateway JWT brand validation](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/services/api-gateway/src/middleware/auth.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L221-L237)

The gateway rejects a brand mismatch only when `tokenBrand` is defined.

Consequently, a token with no brand claim can pass this particular check if its signature, audience, token type and other requirements are satisfied.

That is inconsistent with the intended strict brand isolation model.

Assessment: Confirmed missing-claim acceptance at the gateway check. A cross-brand exploit is not established; downstream checks and token-issuer constraints must still be considered.

## 5. SU-GATEWAY-005 — Untrusted identity headers can survive on public routes

P1 — Trust-boundary verification

[Gateway proxy header construction](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/services/api-gateway/src/lib/proxy.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L44-L103)

The gateway copies incoming headers into a new `Headers` object and overwrites identity headers only when corresponding verified identity values are supplied.

For a public route, those verified values are generally absent. The original client-supplied identity headers can therefore remain in the forwarded request.

Confirmed: The proxy does not universally strip incoming `X-User-ID`, `X-Shadow-User-ID`, `X-Original-User-ID`, `X-User-Roles` and `X-Portal-Identity` before constructing trusted upstream headers.

Critical follow-up: Identify every downstream handler that trusts those headers without verifying the gateway's internal secret. The presence of the headers alone must never establish identity.

## 6. SU-GATEWAY-006 — Internal secret is forwarded to upstream services

[Internal-secret forwarding](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/services/api-gateway/src/lib/proxy.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L66-L78)

The proxy forwards the internal gateway secret to upstream services. This is consistent with a service-to-service trust design.

But because the same secret participates in request trust, its exposure would have a wide blast radius. It needs centralized configuration, limited access, rotation and clear separation from browser-facing headers.

# Principal Architect Audit — Identity Bridge and API Gateway Trust

This tranche reviewed six more files, including the identity bridge, API server gateway guard and targeted tests. The review reveals an important distinction: some previously identified risks are mitigated by the API server, but the trust boundary is not yet consistently enforced.

## SU-IDENTITY-004 — Identity bridge operations are not atomic

P1 — Data integrity

In [UserIdentityBridgeService.ts, lines 53–83](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/identity-bridge/src/UserIdentityBridgeService.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L53-L83), creating a new shadow identity involves two separate database writes:

1. Insert the user into the People database.
2. Insert that user's platform-access record.

These operations are not wrapped in a database transaction.

Confirmed failure mode: If the first insert succeeds and the second fails, the database can retain a shadow user without the intended platform-access record.

A subsequent synchronization finds the existing user and returns immediately without restoring missing platform access.

Required correction: Make identity creation and platform-access assignment transactional, and ensure existing identities are reconciled against their required access records.

## SU-IDENTITY-005 — Identity synchronization can change a shared user's email

[Existing-user synchronization](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/identity-bridge/src/UserIdentityBridgeService.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L20-L50)

When a matching shadow user exists, the bridge updates the user's email directly from the incoming brand identity.

The People schema has a unique email constraint. This can produce synchronization failures when two different brand identities use the same email address.

There is also an ownership question: should a brand identity synchronization be allowed to overwrite an authoritative global email?

Priority: P1 — identity ownership and consistency. The approved architecture must determine which system owns canonical email changes.

## SU-GATEWAY-007 — API server exposes prefixes of internal secrets in logs

P1 — Secret handling

In [gateway-auth.middleware.ts, lines 74–110](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/middleware/gateway-auth.middleware.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L74-L110), invalid-secret logging includes the first ten characters of both the received and expected secret.

This is unnecessary disclosure of secret material into operational logs.

Confirmed: The code logs secret prefixes on failed authentication attempts.

Required correction: Log only non-sensitive metadata such as request ID, route, credential type and rejection reason. Never log any part of the secret itself.

## SU-GATEWAY-008 — Public authentication endpoints bypass the internal gateway-secret check

[Gateway authentication exemptions](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/middleware/gateway-auth.middleware.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L32-L51)

The API server deliberately exempts health endpoints and several public authentication endpoints, including login, signup and password reset.

This is not necessarily a defect: public authentication endpoints must be reachable before a user has a JWT.

However, the source comment states that all direct API access is forbidden. The implementation does not enforce that rule for the exempt endpoints.

Assessment: Confirmed mismatch between the documented gateway-only policy and the middleware's exemptions. Whether this creates a real bypass depends on network exposure, rate limiting and the individual endpoint protections.

Priority: P2 — architecture and deployment verification.

## SU-GATEWAY-009 — Header trust must be checked beyond the gateway-secret guard

The API server's gateway middleware verifies a shared secret before allowing protected requests. That is a useful control.

But a valid gateway secret authenticates the calling service, not automatically the end user represented by forwarded identity headers.

The earlier proxy review found that client-supplied identity headers are not universally removed before forwarding.

Together, these findings establish a trust-boundary concern: a request can arrive through the legitimate gateway while still carrying identity headers originally supplied by a client.

Required verification: Every downstream consumer of `x-user-id`, `x-original-user-id`, `x-shadow-user-id`, `x-user-roles` and `x-portal-identity` must be inventoried. Protected handlers must use authenticated identity rather than assuming that any header arriving with a gateway secret was generated by the gateway.

Priority: P1 — security verification.

## SU-TEST-005 — Identity bridge tests do not cover partial database failures

[Identity bridge test suite](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/identity-bridge/src/__tests__/bridge.service.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The existing tests cover new-user creation, existing-user reuse, brand/platform mismatch and lookup behavior.

Those are useful baseline tests.

The reviewed suite does not cover transaction rollback, concurrent identity creation, unique-email conflicts, failed platform-access inserts or recovery of incomplete identity records.

## SU-TEST-006 — Gateway proxy tests omit malicious identity headers

[Gateway proxy test suite](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/services/api-gateway/src/lib/__tests__/proxy.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The test checks trusted hostname propagation and removal of the `Expect` header.

It does not test whether incoming identity or role headers are removed or overwritten on public routes.

A useful negative test would supply forged identity headers to a public gateway route and assert that none are forwarded as trusted identity.

## SU-TEST-007 — Refresh tests do not assert restored authorization claims

[Token refresh coverage tests](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/__tests__/token-refresh.service.coverage.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The two reviewed tests verify that the appropriate refresh-token verifier is called.

They do not assert the roles, email, brand or identity claims supplied to the newly generated access token.

This explains why the previously confirmed refresh-role defect can remain undetected by these tests.

### Principal Architect checkpoint

The most consequential newly confirmed implementation issue is non-atomic shadow-user creation, because identity records and platform-access records can become inconsistent.

The highest-priority security items across the ongoing audit remain session ownership enforcement, identity-header trust, brand isolation and refresh-token correctness.

The next source-review tranche should examine the actual downstream consumers of gateway identity headers and the session/token repository's concurrency controls. Those are the dependencies needed to establish the full security impact.

No files were changed, no tests were executed, and the full repository audit remains in progress.

# Principal Architect Audit — Internal Authentication and Repository Tests

This tranche adds four more files to the reviewed inventory. The most important result is that the API server's internal authentication middleware does check shared secrets, but that protection is not sufficient if the gateway forwards identity headers supplied by the client.

## SU-GATEWAY-010 — Service authentication and end-user authentication are conflated

P1 — Trust boundary

Source: [Internal authentication middleware](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/middleware/internal-auth.middleware.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L51-L129).

The `validateRequest()` function accepts a matching `x-internal-secret`, then constructs an authenticated context using `x-user-id`, `x-brand` and `x-user-roles`.

It does not independently verify the identity represented by those headers.

That design can be secure only if every service allowed to supply the internal secret also guarantees that identity headers were generated from verified credentials.

The gateway proxy reviewed previously does not always provide that guarantee: it begins with the client's headers and only overwrites identity fields when verified values are available.

This establishes a concrete trust-boundary weakness across the two implementations. Whether a specific endpoint is exploitable still depends on its routing and middleware composition.

Required remediation design: Strip all incoming privileged identity headers at the public gateway boundary. Reconstruct them exclusively from verified JWT claims, and distinguish service identity from end-user identity.

## SU-GATEWAY-011 — Two internal-secret configuration contracts coexist

The reviewed middleware uses:

- `INTERNAL_API_SECRET` for `x-internal-secret`.
- `GATEWAY_TRUST_SECRET` for `x-gateway-secret`.

The separate `gateway-auth.middleware.ts` uses `INTERNAL_API_SECRET` and `INTERNAL_GATEWAY_SECRET`.

That means the two middleware implementations do not agree on the legacy gateway-secret environment variable.

Priority: P1 — configuration consistency. This can produce environment-dependent authentication failures or inconsistent trust enforcement. We need to inventory which routes invoke each middleware before determining the actual impact.

## SU-SESSION-003 — Session repository does not enforce ownership as an invariant

Source: [TokenRepository.revokeById()](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/repositories/token.repository.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L58-L70).

The repository documents `revokeById()` as user-scoped, but the `userId` argument remains optional.

That is the underlying reason the previously identified cross-user session-revocation defect is possible.

The reviewed repository test actually calls `revokeById('rt1')` without a user ID and expects success.

This is a particularly important test-design issue: the test preserves the insecure contract rather than rejecting it.

Priority: P0 remediation candidate. The eventual change must enforce ownership at both the service and repository layers, with negative tests for mismatched owners.

## SU-SESSION-004 — Session lookups use inconsistent validity rules

Source: [Session lookup methods](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/repositories/token.repository.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L104-L141).

`findValidToken()` and `findValidSession()` check ownership, revocation and expiration.

`findByHash()` checks revocation but does not check expiration.

This may be intentional because callers sometimes need to inspect expired records. But it means callers must not assume `findByHash()` returns an active session.

Priority: P2 — API contract clarity. The method names and return types should distinguish lookup from validity verification.

## SU-TEST-008 — Gateway security tests do not cover authenticated header laundering

Source: [Gateway trust tests](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/middleware/__tests__/gateway-01.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

The existing tests correctly check missing secrets, incorrect secrets, unsupported brands and direct spoofed user headers.

But they do not simulate the critical combined scenario:

A public request supplies forged identity headers, the legitimate gateway forwards them with its own internal secret, and the API server interprets those headers as authenticated user context.

That cross-component scenario needs a regression test.

## SU-TEST-009 — Token repository tests omit owner-isolation assertions

Source: [Token repository tests](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/repositories/__tests__/token.repository.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

The reviewed test exercises create, revoke, touch and lookup methods, but it does not assert the generated database predicate or verify that one user cannot revoke another user's session.

Required test: An authenticated user attempting to revoke a session belonging to a different user must produce no mutation, regardless of whether the session ID is known.

## Additional file findings

`request-context.ts` is a small observability utility. It generates request IDs and does not itself establish authorization. No significant security defect was established in its reviewed logic.

`blockDirectAccess()` in `internal-auth.middleware.ts` deliberately allows JWT-bearing requests to proceed to subsequent verification. That is acceptable only when the subsequent verification actually occurs; the function alone does not authenticate a JWT.

# Principal Architect Audit — API Server Route Enforcement

This tranche exposes an important gap between the API server's central authentication policy and the checks performed by individual routes.

## SU-AUTH-020 — Broad route exemptions weaken central authentication enforcement

P1 — Authorization coverage

Source: [API server proxy, lines 47–81](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/proxy.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L47-L81).

The API server excludes entire route families from its central JWT verification, including `/api/auth`, `/api/tutorial`, workflow routes and several other prefixes.

These exemptions may be intentional because individual handlers perform their own authentication.

However, the implementation makes security dependent on each exempt route doing that correctly.

Confirmed: Central JWT verification does not cover those route families.

Not yet confirmed: That an individual protected endpoint is accessible without authentication.

The required next step is a route-by-route authorization matrix, identifying the exact guard used by every exempt endpoint.

## SU-AUTH-021 — `logout-all` uses a session validator that does not validate session state

Source: [Logout-all route](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/app/api/auth/logout-all/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L26-L36).

This route calls `authMiddleware.requireValidSession()` before revoking sessions.

The previously reviewed implementation of `requireValidSession()` verifies the JWT but leaves session-repository validation unimplemented.

Confirmed: The logout-all route relies on a misleadingly named session guard.

This does not automatically allow cross-user logout: the route still derives its user ID from the verified token. But it may accept a valid access token even when its underlying session has already been revoked.

Priority: P1 — session revocation semantics.

## SU-AUTH-022 — The `/me` endpoint can accept a different active session

Source: [Current-user session validation](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/app/api/auth/me/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L136-L174).

The `/me` endpoint has a strong path: when a refresh-token cookie exists, it hashes that token and checks the corresponding session for the authenticated user.

However, when the refresh-token cookie is absent, it falls back to checking whether the user has any active refresh-token session.

That means a valid access token without its corresponding refresh cookie may still pass `/me` because another device has an active session.

Confirmed: The fallback checks account-level session existence rather than the requesting device's session.

Priority: P1 — session identity correctness. The desired behavior should be explicitly specified for missing refresh cookies, expired refresh cookies and revoked sessions.

## SU-CSRF-001 — Origin validation uses substring matching

P1 — Security validation

Source: [CSRF middleware, lines 31–43](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/csrf.middleware.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L31-L43).

The CSRF middleware considers an origin allowed when either it appears in the configured allowlist or:

```
origin.includes(host ?? '')
```

Substring matching is not a safe way to compare origins and hosts. A hostname embedded within another hostname can satisfy this expression.

The middleware also checks a CSRF cookie against a request header, which provides a separate protective layer. Therefore, this finding does not establish a complete CSRF bypass.

Required correction: Compare parsed, canonical origins against an explicit allowlist, with a defined policy for trusted reverse proxies.

## SU-CSRF-002 — Missing `Origin` is accepted if the CSRF token matches

The same middleware rejects a disallowed origin only when the `Origin` header is present.

A missing origin is not itself rejected, although the CSRF cookie/header equality check still applies.

This may be appropriate for some non-browser clients. The required policy should distinguish browser cookie authentication from trusted machine-to-machine requests.

Priority: P2 — policy clarification and negative testing.

## SU-TEST-010 — Authentication exemptions need a route-level verification matrix

The reviewed `proxy.ts` contains multiple exemptions, and the `/me` and `logout-all` routes demonstrate why a central policy alone is insufficient to certify authorization.

The audit should record, for each endpoint, the authentication mechanism, expected audience, brand validation, authorization check, identity source and CSRF behavior.

This will allow us to identify actual unprotected endpoints rather than treating every exemption as a vulnerability.

# Principal Architect Audit — Session Services, CSRF Tests and Refresh-Token Persistence

I continued the read-only audit with five additional files. This tranche reveals an architectural inconsistency that needs to be resolved before we can trust the logout-all flow.

## SU-SESSION-005 — Two different `SessionService` implementations coexist

P1 — Service contract

The repository contains two separate implementations:

- [API server SessionService](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/session.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — 29 lines, providing `createSession()`, `revokeRefreshTokens()` and `cleanExpiredSessions()`.
- [Shared authentication SessionService](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/auth/src/session.service.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — a separate service with its own repository contract.

The logout-all endpoint imports the shared implementation, while other API-server code uses its local session implementation.

This creates two distinct abstractions for session management, with different methods and persistence assumptions.

Confirmed: Both implementations exist and the logout-all route selects the shared one.

Still requiring verification: Whether the dependency-injection container registers the shared service correctly, and whether its repository implementation revokes the same brand-specific refresh-token records used during login.

This is an architecture consistency issue, not yet proof that logout-all fails at runtime.

## SU-TEST-011 — Refresh tests reinforce an unsafe repository call pattern

Source: [Refresh branch test](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/__tests__/auth.refresh.branch.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L42-L53).

The test explicitly expects:

```
expect(mockTokenRepo.revokeById).toHaveBeenCalledWith('s1');
```

This is another test that assumes `revokeById()` may be called without a user-owner argument.

Unlike the single-session deletion defect, refresh rotation may already have verified the token's ownership before reaching this call. Nevertheless, the repository contract should not permit unscoped revocation.

Priority: P1 — security contract and test alignment.

## SU-TEST-012 — CSRF tests omit lookalike-hostname attacks

Source: [CSRF middleware tests](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/__tests__/csrf.middleware.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

The tests cover safe methods, missing tokens, matching cookie/header tokens, trusted internal keys and an obviously unrelated origin.

However, they do not cover the exact weakness identified in `origin.includes(host)`.

For example, a test should establish that a request with host `trusted.example` does not accept an origin such as `https://trusted.example.attacker.invalid`, even when the CSRF cookie and header are equal.

This matters because a generic mismatched-origin test does not verify resistance to hostname substring confusion.

Priority: P1 — security regression coverage.

## SU-SESSION-006 — Device-session migration has no session ownership constraint

Source: [Device tracking migration](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db/migrations/0001_add_device_tracking_to_refresh_tokens.sql?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

The migration adds device ID, IP address, user agent, device name and last-used timestamp columns, along with indexes.

It does not introduce a database constraint enforcing session ownership during revocation. That is not necessarily a schema defect: ownership is normally enforced in the mutation's `WHERE` clause.

The important conclusion is that the database migration does not compensate for the missing owner condition in `revokeById()`.

The migration also does not establish refresh-token family or replay-detection behavior.

## SU-TEST-013 — Local session-service tests cover only basic operations

Source: [Session service tests](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/auth/__tests__/session.service.test.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

The three tests verify that a session can be created, refresh tokens can be revoked, and expired sessions can be deleted.

They do not test cross-brand isolation, revoked-session authentication, transaction failures or consistency between the two session-service implementations.
