# SkillUp Principal Architect Audit — Legacy Progress and Migration Safety

Branch: `feature/project-llm-linux-worker` · Read-only source review · Architecture baseline: `FinalAechitecture.md`

This tranche has exposed an important distinction: SkillUp has both a legacy subtopic-progress repository and the newer ILS navigation-progress model. They use different completion rules and persistence mechanisms. That makes it especially important to establish which model is authoritative before recommending consolidation.

## SU-PROGRESS-001 — Legacy progress updates can lose concurrent completions

P1 — Data integrity

Source: [Legacy markBlockComplete implementation](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-tutorial/src/repositories/tutorial-progress.repository.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L60-L116).

The method reads the current row, merges the completed block into an in-memory array, and writes the entire array back.

Two simultaneous requests completing different block types can both read the same original array. Whichever update finishes last may overwrite the other completion.

The numeric `version` field is incremented, but it is not used as an optimistic-lock condition in the update.

Confirmed: The method uses a non-atomic read–modify–write pattern.

Recommended action: Use an atomic database update or version-checked retry. This should be coordinated with the decision about retiring or retaining the legacy progress model.

## SU-PROGRESS-002 — The legacy progress table has no soft-delete-aware unique index

P2 — Lifecycle consistency

Source: [Legacy progress uniqueness](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-tutorial/src/schema/tutorial-progress.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L20-L23).

The unique index covers `(user_id, subtopic_id)` without excluding soft-deleted rows.

The newer navigation-progress table uses a partial unique index restricted to active records.

Confirmed: The two models have different soft-delete and recreation semantics.

Recommendation: Decide whether legacy progress rows are intended to be restorable or recreatable, and align the schema with that policy.

## SU-PROGRESS-003 — Reset and initial creation are vulnerable to request races

Source: [Reset progress implementation](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-tutorial/src/repositories/tutorial-progress.repository.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L146-L192).

`resetProgress()` first checks for a row and then either inserts or updates it. `markBlockComplete()` follows a similar check-then-insert approach.

Concurrent first-time requests can race on the unique key. A reset can also interleave with a completion update.

Confirmed: There is no explicit conflict-safe insert or transaction-level coordination in these methods.

Priority: P1 — verify active callers and intended reset semantics.

## SU-MIGRATION-002 — Destructive telemetry repair script lacks a production safety gate

P1 — Operational safety

Source: [Telemetry table deletion script](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-tutorial/scripts/drop-old-telemetry-table.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L34-L113).

The script checks whether `block_telemetry_events` exists, displays its columns, and then executes:

```
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS block_telemetry_events CASCADE;
```

Although the comments describe an old table with incorrect column types, the code does not require those incorrect types to be present before deleting the table.

It also has no visible environment allowlist, explicit operator confirmation or backup prerequisite.

Confirmed: Running this script against a database containing a valid telemetry table could delete its event history and dependent objects.

Recommendation: Remove it from ordinary operational workflows or require an explicit nonproduction environment gate, exact schema preconditions and a documented recovery procedure.

No script was executed during this audit.

## SU-MIGRATION-003 — Raw migration runner bypasses normal migration tracking

P1 — Deployment consistency

Source: [Raw migration runner](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-tutorial/src/run-raw-migration.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L24-L79).

This script reads migration `0018_amused_rockslide.sql`, splits its SQL statements, and executes them individually.

It ignores errors based on message text such as `already exists` or `duplicate key value`.

Confirmed: The runner does not update the normal Drizzle migration journal and does not visibly wrap all statements in one transaction.

Potential impact: A database could be partially migrated while appearing successfully processed by this custom script.

Recommendation: Treat this as a controlled recovery utility, not a normal migration path. Prefer versioned migrations with explicit preconditions and post-migration verification.

## SU-MIGRATION-004 — Telemetry uniqueness is established in migration SQL

Source: [Telemetry table migration](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-tutorial/migrations/0025_quiet_tenebrous.sql?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L1-L15).

Migration `0025` creates `block_telemetry_events` and declares a unique index on `event_id`.

This confirms that the repository's idempotent event-claiming strategy has a corresponding database migration.

Positive finding: The telemetry uniqueness invariant is represented in actual migration SQL, not just the TypeScript schema.

Remaining verification: Whether that migration was successfully applied to the relevant SkillUp database.

## SU-MIGRATION-005 — Database counters have no explicit nonnegative checks in the reviewed migrations

Sources: [Navigation progress migration](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-tutorial/migrations/0022_broken_supernaut.sql?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [Block state migration](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-tutorial/migrations/0023_lame_deathbird.sql?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and [Telemetry migration](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/packages/db-tutorial/migrations/0025_quiet_tenebrous.sql?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

These migrations create integer fields for visit counts, revision counts and active time without declaring `CHECK` constraints that enforce nonnegative values.

Confirmed: Those original migrations lack the constraints.

Not yet confirmed: Whether later SQL or manual migrations add them.

Priority: P2 — database defense in depth.

## Assessment against FinalAechitecture.md

| Principle               | Assessment                                                                               |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| SOLID                   | Progress interfaces and repository responsibilities are reasonably separated             |
| DRY                     | Two progress models create overlapping domain responsibilities                           |
| KISS                    | The newer atomic SQL approach is simpler to reason about under concurrency               |
| YAGNI                   | Do not introduce a third progress abstraction; first determine the authoritative model   |
| Data integrity          | Legacy read–modify–write updates need attention                                          |
| Security                | Authenticated identity contracts are explicit, but session ownership remains unresolved  |
| Operational reliability | Destructive repair and raw migration utilities require stronger safeguards               |
| Testability             | Legacy tests verify expected outputs but do not reproduce concurrent database operations |

## Principal Architect conclusion

This tranche strengthens the evidence that the legacy progress implementation and newer ILS implementation do not provide equivalent concurrency guarantees.

The highest-priority decisions are to identify the authoritative progress model, establish session ownership, and protect database maintenance operations from accidental destructive execution.

I would next trace the SkillUp API consumers of `TutorialProgressRepository` and `LearningProgressService`. That will show whether the legacy concurrency risks affect active learner journeys, and whether the two systems can produce conflicting dashboard or completion states.

No files were changed. No tests, migrations, database commands, commits or deployments were executed.

## Confirmed: SkillUp's active API exposes two different progress contracts

The current SkillUp BFF has two separate learner-facing routes:

- `/api/tutorial/progress` uses the legacy `TutorialProgressRepository` and a section-type completion calculation.
- `/api/tutorial/ils/subtopic/[subtopicId]/progress` uses the newer `LearningProgressService`, which evaluates navigation nodes and versioned blocks.

These are not interchangeable representations of the same data. One tracks completed section types; the other tracks individual navigation nodes and block versions.

That is an important bounded-context and single-source-of-truth concern under `FinalAechitecture.md`. We still need to trace which frontend components and dashboard calculations consume each route before declaring either one obsolete.

## Further confirmed findings — Tutorial Engine and SkillUp Dashboard

### SU-BRAND-001 — Legacy Tutorial Engine's brand authorization always succeeds

P1 — Brand isolation

Source: [Brand-access validation](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/tutorial-engine/tutorial.engine.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L204-L220).

`validateBrandAccess()` contains a TODO describing the intended brand-exclusivity rules, but the implementation simply returns `true`.

Both content retrieval and progress tracking call this method.

Confirmed: This method enforces no brand restriction.

Conditional exposure: Whether a learner can actually access another brand's content depends on upstream authentication, repository filtering and route exposure. Those controls must be traced before asserting an exploitable cross-brand leak.

Recommendation: Enforce brand authorization using the canonical content-visibility contract, and test SkillUp, RTH and shared-content cases.

### SU-PROGRESS-004 — Legacy and ILS progress can disagree

P1 — Single source of truth

Source: [Legacy progress tracking](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/tutorial-engine/tutorial.engine.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L158-L189).

The legacy engine calls `TutorialProgressRepository.markBlockComplete()`.

The newer ILS endpoints call `LearningProgressService` and use `tutorial_navigation_progress` plus block-level state.

Confirmed: These are separate persistence paths with different completion rules.

Risk: A learner may appear complete in one view and incomplete in another unless an explicit synchronization or projection contract exists.

Recommendation: Establish one authoritative completion policy and define how legacy consumers transition to it. Do not simply delete the older table.

### SU-TUTORIAL-006 — Legacy brand-specific content customizations may be applied to the wrong source record

Source: [Content retrieval](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/tutorial-engine/tutorial.engine.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L116-L145).

The engine calls `getPublished(subtopicId, difficulty)` and selects the first returned content record before applying brand customizations.

Confirmed: The engine does not pass `brandId` into this repository call.

Verification required: Whether `getPublished()` returns only shared content or performs some other brand filtering internally.

### SU-TUTORIAL-007 — Remediation is a logging placeholder

Source: [Remediation implementation](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/api-server/src/modules/tutorial-engine/tutorial.engine.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L279-L297).

`needsRemediation()` computes the remediation flag, but `triggerRemediation()` only writes a log entry.

Confirmed: The legacy engine does not create a remediation record or notify a learner through this method.

Priority: P2, subject to whether the legacy remediation workflow remains supported.

### SU-DASHBOARD-001 — SkillUp dashboard progress measures sessions, not tutorial mastery

Source: [Student dashboard metrics](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/lib/skillup-data.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com#L248-L291).

The dashboard calculates `progressPercent` from completed batch sessions divided by scheduled sessions.

This is distinct from both the legacy tutorial progress percentage and ILS navigation progress.

Confirmed: The dashboard metric is session-based.

Architectural implication: It should be labelled as session or batch progress, not assumed to represent tutorial mastery. If the product intends an overall learning-progress metric, it needs an explicit aggregation contract.

## Principal Architect conclusion

We now have direct evidence of three distinct meanings of progress in SkillUp:

1. Legacy tutorial section completion.
2. ILS navigation-node and versioned-block completion.
3. Batch-session completion shown on the SkillUp dashboard.

These may legitimately coexist if they represent explicitly different business concepts. The architectural problem arises when their names, API contracts or user interfaces imply that they are interchangeable.

The highest-priority issue in this tranche is the always-true brand-access method in the legacy Tutorial Engine. The next review should trace its content repository and actual SkillUp frontend callers to establish the effective exposure and the correct domain boundary.

Audit remains strictly read-only. No files were modified, and no tests, migrations, commits or deployments were executed.

## Principal Architect finding: the legacy tutorial content path is not actually brand-aware

I traced:

`SkillUp BFF → API-server legacy TutorialService → TutorialEngine → TutorialContentRepository → tutorial_content schema`

The result is now conclusive.

The legacy `tutorial_content` table contains:

- `subtopicId`
- `difficulty`
- `contentType`
- content/version/language/publication fields
- AI/admin metadata

but **no `brandId` and no `brandVisibility`**.

`TutorialContentRepository.getPublished()` filters only by:

```text
subtopicId
isPublished = true
deletedAt IS NULL
difficulty (optional)
```

It performs **zero brand filtering**.

That changes the status of the earlier finding.

### SU-BRAND-001 — P1 — Legacy brand validation is functionally ineffective

`TutorialEngine.validateBrandAccess()` still simply returns:

```ts
return true;
```

The repository underneath it cannot compensate because `tutorial_content` has no brand ownership fields.

Even more importantly, after retrieving the first result, `TutorialEngine` returns:

```ts
brandId: brandId
```

where `brandId` is the **requested brand**, not a brand read from the content record.

Therefore the downstream API's check:

```text
tutorialBrand === userBrand
```

does not establish content ownership.

Conceptually the current flow is:

```text
request says skillup
        ↓
engine receives skillup
        ↓
repository retrieves brand-blind tutorial_content
        ↓
engine labels returned object "skillup"
        ↓
API compares skillup == skillup
        ↓
PASS
```

That check is tautological.

### Architectural classification

**Confirmed architecture violation. P1.**

However, I am being precise about what it proves.

It does **not automatically prove cross-brand confidential content leakage**, because the old `tutorial_content` model may effectively contain only universal/shared material.

What is proven is:

> the legacy architecture cannot enforce brand-exclusive tutorial ownership because the persistence model itself has no brand discriminator.

That is enough reason not to extend this architecture further.

# A second P1 issue appeared in the same legacy API

This is potentially more immediately dangerous.

The backend legacy route retrieves tutorial content **with learner progress**.

`TutorialEngine.getTutorialContent()` defaults:

```ts
includeProgress = true
```

and then calls:

```text
progressRepo.getProgress(userId, subtopicId)
```

So the returned result contains user-specific progress.

But the API-server route subsequently sends:

```http
Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
```

## SU-CACHE-003 — P1 — Personalized tutorial response marked publicly cacheable

The response can contain:

```text
tutorial content
+
user-specific blocksCompleted
+
completionPercent
+
assignmentUnlocked
```

while declaring itself public-cacheable.

That is architecturally incorrect.

Even though the SkillUp BFF wraps its own browser-facing response with:

```http
Cache-Control: private, no-store
```

the **upstream API response itself** has already been declared public.

Therefore any cache operating between that API route and its consumers could theoretically reuse a response without understanding the user identity encoded only in headers.

The requested URL does not appear to contain the user ID.

Conceptually:

```text
GET /api/tutorial/content/abc
X-User-ID: learner-A

→ response includes learner-A progress
→ Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
```

followed by:

```text
GET /api/tutorial/content/abc
X-User-ID: learner-B
```

could be dangerous if an intermediary cache keys primarily on the URL and ignores the identity header.

I have **not reproduced that runtime scenario**, so I will not claim an observed cross-user leak.

But the cache declaration itself is unquestionably wrong for personalized data.

**Disposition: Must fix or retire the endpoint. P1.**

---

# The newer tutorial architecture is materially better

I then traced:

`tutorial_sections → TutorialSectionRepository → TutorialDeliveryService`

This is a fundamentally different architecture.

The schema explicitly contains:

```text
brandId
brandVisibility
navigationNodeId
status
deletedAt
```

and the active identity is effectively:

```text
subtopic
+
navigation page
+
brand
```

The database even has a partial unique constraint for active tutorials based on that identity.

That is far closer to the target architecture.

## SU-TUTORIAL-V2-001 — Positive — Brand context exists in the persistence model

The new delivery service explicitly filters tutorials using:

```text
brandId = shared
OR
brandId = requested brand
OR
brandVisibility = shared_visible
```

This is the correct architectural location for content visibility.

The old system tries to determine brand access after loading a brand-blind record.

The new system makes brand a property of the authoritative record itself.

That is a very important distinction.

---

# But the new brand query needs one more review

There is a subtle correctness issue.

`TutorialDeliveryService` builds an OR expression equivalent to:

```text
brandId = shared
OR brandId = requestedBrand
OR brandVisibility = shared_visible
```

That means a row could theoretically have:

```text
brandId = realtutorialhub
brandVisibility = shared_visible
```

and become visible to SkillUp.

That may be **exactly what `shared_visible` means**.

If so, correct.

But we need an explicit contract:

```text
shared
    → universally owned

brand exclusive
    → requesting brand only

shared_visible
    → owned by one brand but intentionally consumable by another
```

Until that semantic contract is established, I would not change this condition.

**Disposition: Verify business policy; not presently a defect.**

---

# SU-TUTORIAL-V2-002 — Retrieval is nondeterministic when both shared and brand-specific rows match

This is a new correctness finding.

`TutorialDeliveryService` can match:

```text
brandId = skillup
```

and:

```text
brandId = shared
```

for the same requested page.

Then it does effectively:

```ts
.select(...)
.where(...)
.limit(1)
```

without an explicit ordering giving precedence to the exact brand match.

Similarly, `TutorialSectionRepository.getTutorialByPageIdentity()` allows:

```text
requested brand OR shared
```

and then:

```text
.limit(1)
```

with no deterministic priority.

But its comment says:

> Prioritizes exact brand match
> Falls back to shared

The code as inspected does **not explicitly enforce that priority**.

This is important.

If both exist:

```text
SkillUp-specific content
shared fallback content
```

the query needs deterministic semantics such as:

```text
exact requested brand first
shared second
```

rather than relying on database row order.

### Classification

**SU-TUTORIAL-V2-002 — P1/P2 correctness**

I would classify it P1 if brand-specific content is legally/business materially different; otherwise P2.

This should be resolved before declaring the V2 delivery contract authoritative.

---

# SU-TUTORIAL-V2-003 — Repository comments no longer match schema identity

There are several comments saying:

```text
ONE tutorial per subtopic per brand
```

and:

```text
Identity: (subtopicId, brandId)
```

But the actual current schema has evolved to:

```text
subtopicId
+
navigationNodeId
+
brandId
```

The database's active unique index correctly reflects the newer identity.

So executable schema is ahead of some repository/service documentation.

This doesn't break production directly, but stale architectural comments are dangerous here because this is a core domain identity.

**Disposition: P2 documentation/code coherence cleanup.**

# SU-TUTORIAL-V2-004 — Excessive diagnostic logging remains inside repository writes

`TutorialSectionRepository.createTutorial()` constructs a diagnostic identifier using `Date.now()` and emits multiple `console.log()` statements covering:

```text
subtopic
brand
order
status
version
block count
```

On failure it logs:

```text
database error type
message
code
detail
constraint
table
column
stack
```

That is useful during development but too much low-level persistence diagnostic information for normal production repository behavior.

The repository should normally throw a typed error and let controlled observability capture appropriate details.

### Classification

**P2 — observability / SRP concern**

Not security-critical by itself, but worth cleaning as part of production hardening.

---

# SU-TUTORIAL-V2-005 — `any` weakens an otherwise strongly typed repository

The new repository repeatedly uses patterns like:

```ts
brandId as any
```

and:

```ts
const updateData: any = ...
```

That weakens precisely the part of the architecture where explicit contracts are valuable.

Examples include:

```text
brand identity
status transitions
TutorialDocument persistence
update structures
```

The architecture should derive these types from the Drizzle schema or explicit domain types.

I would not create a hierarchy of interfaces purely for SOLID; simply removing unnecessary `any` would give us more value with less complexity.

**Classification: P2 — type-safety weakness.**

# New architecture vs legacy architecture

We can now make a much stronger architectural decision.

| Concern | Legacy `tutorial_content` | V2 `tutorial_sections` |
|---|---|---|
| Brand stored in record | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Brand visibility contract | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Navigation-page identity | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Soft deletion | ✅ | ✅ |
| Publication lifecycle | Simple boolean | Explicit statuses |
| Learner-safe sanitization | ❌ Not demonstrated | ✅ Present |
| Content schema validation on delivery | Weak/legacy cast | ✅ `TutorialDocumentSchema` |
| Brand filtering during query | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Supports current ILS model | Legacy | Designed for it |
| Architecture direction | Retire | Preserve/evolve |

My Principal Architect recommendation therefore changes from:

> “Implement brand filtering in the legacy engine.”

to:

> **Do not invest heavily in making the legacy `tutorial_content` engine a second correct brand-aware content architecture unless active callers require a transitional fix. The correct long-term authority should be `tutorial_sections` + `TutorialDeliveryService`.**

That respects KISS, YAGNI and single ownership.

# Progress architecture review expanded

I also reviewed the legacy `TutorialProgressRepository`.

It has a database unique index on:

```text
(userId, subtopicId)
```

which is positive.

But `markBlockComplete()` follows:

```text
read existing row
        ↓
compute merged blocks in application memory
        ↓
update row
```

This is not equivalent to the newer ILS atomic SQL model.

Two concurrent completion requests can potentially read the same old `blocksCompleted` value and write competing updates.

The `version` field is incremented:

```text
version = version + 1
```

but the update does **not compare an expected version**.

Therefore the version counter is not optimistic concurrency control.

### SU-PROGRESS-005 — P1/P2 — Legacy progress can lose concurrent completions

Conceptually:

```text
existing = [notes]

Request A reads [notes]
Request B reads [notes]

A adds code
→ [notes, code]

B adds technical
→ [notes, technical]
```

Depending on ordering, one update can overwrite the other.

The newer ILS database helpers previously reviewed use much stronger atomic database expressions.

This is another reason to avoid maintaining two authoritative progress systems.

---

# Interaction routes: secure scoring improved, progress architecture still broken

I also re-reviewed the current quiz/practice/completion interaction path.

There is an important positive:

## SU-INTERACTION-001 — Positive — Quiz and practice answers are server-authoritative

Both quiz and practice now derive the answer from stored tutorial section content using:

```text
extractCorrectAnswerFromContent(section.content, questionId)
```

If an authoritative answer cannot be found:

```http
422
```

is returned.

Client-provided `correctAnswer` is no longer scoring authority.

That remediation should be preserved.

---

# But the comments are stale

The quiz header comment still describes an older strategy involving:

```text
previous correct answer
or client fallback on first attempt
```

while the executable implementation correctly does neither.

Practice has similar stale commentary.

### SU-CODE-DOC-001 — P2

Security comments contradict the current secure implementation.

This matters because future maintainers could “fix” the code back toward the obsolete behavior after reading misleading comments.

**Disposition: update comments during remediation, without changing current scoring authority.**

---

# SU-INTERACTION-002 remains confirmed — returned progress is fake/placeholder

The shared helper:

```ts
updateProgressForSection(...)
```

does not inspect actual progress.

It returns:

```text
calculateTutorialProgress({
    completedSections: []
})
```

Every caller therefore receives progress equivalent to an empty completion state.

So after a learner successfully answers a quiz or finishes an interaction:

```text
database interaction record
        ✅ real
progress returned in same response
        ❌ placeholder
```

This is not merely technical debt if frontend code consumes that response.

### Classification

**P1 if active UI relies on it.**

The correct solution is not to add more logic here.

The interaction API should use the canonical ILS progress application service, or stop returning misleading progress altogether during migration.

---

# SU-INTERACTION-004 — Attempt numbering race remains

Quiz and practice calculate:

```text
existing attempts
        ↓
length + 1
        ↓
insert
```

That is a standard concurrency race.

Two simultaneous submissions can both calculate:

```text
attemptNumber = 3
```

unless a database constraint prevents it.

I attempted to inspect the corresponding schema paths, but those schema filenames are not at the conventional paths I tried, so I am **not yet claiming database constraints are absent**.

Current status:

**Code-level race confirmed. Database-level protection still unverified.**

---

# SU-INTERACTION-005 — Quiz score meaning is problematic

The GET endpoint computes:

```ts
correctAnswers / totalAttempts * 100
```

while reporting:

```text
totalQuestions = count(distinct questionIds attempted)
```

Those represent different denominators/concepts.

A learner who attempts one question ten times and succeeds once receives:

```text
totalQuestions: 1
totalAttempts: 10
correctAnswers: 1
score: 10
```

That may be useful as an **attempt accuracy rate**.

It is not necessarily a quiz score.

### Recommendation

Define these separately:

```text
question completion
latest-answer correctness
first-attempt correctness
attempt accuracy
assessment score
```

Do not overload them into one ambiguous `score`.

**Classification: P1/P2 business-contract issue depending on downstream use.**

---

# SU-INTERACTION-007 — Correct answers are written to logs

When the browser submits a mismatched `correctAnswer`, quiz/practice currently log both:

```text
clientValue
authoritativeValue
```

The server should certainly detect tampering.

But logging the authoritative answer key is unnecessary.

For an education/assessment system, answer keys are sensitive application data.

Log instead:

```text
questionId
mismatch = true
request/correlation ID
possibly learner identifier hash
```

not the correct answer.

**Classification: P2 assessment confidentiality.**

---

# Completion route also remains architecturally legacy

`completion/route.ts`:

1. authenticates,
2. validates its JSON,
3. loads a section,
4. checks whether a completion row exists,
5. inserts if it doesn't,
6. returns placeholder progress.

Two issues remain.

### SU-COMPLETION-001 — P1 conditional — Client controls `timeSpent` and `score`

The handler persists browser-provided:

```text
timeSpent
score
```

without deriving them from authoritative learning telemetry.

That could be acceptable if they are explicitly **untrusted analytics metadata**.

It is not acceptable if they drive:

```text
official progress
certificate eligibility
mastery
assessment grading
```

We need to trace their consumers.

---

### SU-COMPLETION-002 — Check-then-insert race

The pattern is:

```text
SELECT completion
if none:
    INSERT completion
```

Two requests can race.

I have not yet verified the underlying unique constraint, so current classification is:

**Concurrency weakness confirmed; effective duplicate risk pending schema verification.**

# One major architecture direction is now clear

We currently have essentially two generations:

```text
LEGACY
tutorial_content
TutorialEngine
TutorialProgressRepository
interaction placeholder progress
section completion records
```

versus:

```text
CURRENT / ILS
tutorial_sections
TutorialDeliveryService
LearningProgressService
navigation progress
block learning state
telemetry
```

Trying to make both equally authoritative would violate:

- DRY
- KISS
- single ownership
- separation of concerns
- change safety

The correct question is no longer:

> “How do we perfectly repair every legacy tutorial class?”

It is:

> **“Which active learner journeys still depend on the legacy system, and what is the minimum safe transition necessary to move those callers onto the V2/ILS authority?”**

That is the architecture decision I recommend.

## Principal Architect finding: the legacy tutorial content path is not actually brand-aware

I traced:

`SkillUp BFF → API-server legacy TutorialService → TutorialEngine → TutorialContentRepository → tutorial_content schema`

The result is now conclusive.

The legacy `tutorial_content` table contains:

- `subtopicId`
- `difficulty`
- `contentType`
- content/version/language/publication fields
- AI/admin metadata

but **no `brandId` and no `brandVisibility`**.

`TutorialContentRepository.getPublished()` filters only by:

```text
subtopicId
isPublished = true
deletedAt IS NULL
difficulty (optional)
```

It performs **zero brand filtering**.

That changes the status of the earlier finding.

### SU-BRAND-001 — P1 — Legacy brand validation is functionally ineffective

`TutorialEngine.validateBrandAccess()` still simply returns:

```ts
return true;
```

The repository underneath it cannot compensate because `tutorial_content` has no brand ownership fields.

Even more importantly, after retrieving the first result, `TutorialEngine` returns:

```ts
brandId: brandId
```

where `brandId` is the **requested brand**, not a brand read from the content record.

Therefore the downstream API's check:

```text
tutorialBrand === userBrand
```

does not establish content ownership.

Conceptually the current flow is:

```text
request says skillup
        ↓
engine receives skillup
        ↓
repository retrieves brand-blind tutorial_content
        ↓
engine labels returned object "skillup"
        ↓
API compares skillup == skillup
        ↓
PASS
```

That check is tautological.

### Architectural classification

**Confirmed architecture violation. P1.**

However, I am being precise about what it proves.

It does **not automatically prove cross-brand confidential content leakage**, because the old `tutorial_content` model may effectively contain only universal/shared material.

What is proven is:

> the legacy architecture cannot enforce brand-exclusive tutorial ownership because the persistence model itself has no brand discriminator.

That is enough reason not to extend this architecture further.

---

# A second P1 issue appeared in the same legacy API

This is potentially more immediately dangerous.

The backend legacy route retrieves tutorial content **with learner progress**.

`TutorialEngine.getTutorialContent()` defaults:

```ts
includeProgress = true
```

and then calls:

```text
progressRepo.getProgress(userId, subtopicId)
```

So the returned result contains user-specific progress.

But the API-server route subsequently sends:

```http
Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
```

## SU-CACHE-003 — P1 — Personalized tutorial response marked publicly cacheable

The response can contain:

```text
tutorial content
+
user-specific blocksCompleted
+
completionPercent
+
assignmentUnlocked
```

while declaring itself public-cacheable.

That is architecturally incorrect.

Even though the SkillUp BFF wraps its own browser-facing response with:

```http
Cache-Control: private, no-store
```

the **upstream API response itself** has already been declared public.

Therefore any cache operating between that API route and its consumers could theoretically reuse a response without understanding the user identity encoded only in headers.

The requested URL does not appear to contain the user ID.

Conceptually:

```text
GET /api/tutorial/content/abc
X-User-ID: learner-A

→ response includes learner-A progress
→ Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
```

followed by:

```text
GET /api/tutorial/content/abc
X-User-ID: learner-B
```

could be dangerous if an intermediary cache keys primarily on the URL and ignores the identity header.

I have **not reproduced that runtime scenario**, so I will not claim an observed cross-user leak.

But the cache declaration itself is unquestionably wrong for personalized data.

**Disposition: Must fix or retire the endpoint. P1.**

---

# The newer tutorial architecture is materially better

I then traced:

`tutorial_sections → TutorialSectionRepository → TutorialDeliveryService`

This is a fundamentally different architecture.

The schema explicitly contains:

```text
brandId
brandVisibility
navigationNodeId
status
deletedAt
```

and the active identity is effectively:

```text
subtopic
+
navigation page
+
brand
```

The database even has a partial unique constraint for active tutorials based on that identity.

That is far closer to the target architecture.

## SU-TUTORIAL-V2-001 — Positive — Brand context exists in the persistence model

The new delivery service explicitly filters tutorials using:

```text
brandId = shared
OR
brandId = requested brand
OR
brandVisibility = shared_visible
```

This is the correct architectural location for content visibility.

The old system tries to determine brand access after loading a brand-blind record.

The new system makes brand a property of the authoritative record itself.

That is a very important distinction.

---

# But the new brand query needs one more review

There is a subtle correctness issue.

`TutorialDeliveryService` builds an OR expression equivalent to:

```text
brandId = shared
OR brandId = requestedBrand
OR brandVisibility = shared_visible
```

That means a row could theoretically have:

```text
brandId = realtutorialhub
brandVisibility = shared_visible
```

and become visible to SkillUp.

That may be **exactly what `shared_visible` means**.

If so, correct.

But we need an explicit contract:

```text
shared
    → universally owned

brand exclusive
    → requesting brand only

shared_visible
    → owned by one brand but intentionally consumable by another
```

Until that semantic contract is established, I would not change this condition.

**Disposition: Verify business policy; not presently a defect.**

---

# SU-TUTORIAL-V2-002 — Retrieval is nondeterministic when both shared and brand-specific rows match

This is a new correctness finding.

`TutorialDeliveryService` can match:

```text
brandId = skillup
```

and:

```text
brandId = shared
```

for the same requested page.

Then it does effectively:

```ts
.select(...)
.where(...)
.limit(1)
```

without an explicit ordering giving precedence to the exact brand match.

Similarly, `TutorialSectionRepository.getTutorialByPageIdentity()` allows:

```text
requested brand OR shared
```

and then:

```text
.limit(1)
```

with no deterministic priority.

But its comment says:

> Prioritizes exact brand match
> Falls back to shared

The code as inspected does **not explicitly enforce that priority**.

This is important.

If both exist:

```text
SkillUp-specific content
shared fallback content
```

the query needs deterministic semantics such as:

```text
exact requested brand first
shared second
```

rather than relying on database row order.

### Classification

**SU-TUTORIAL-V2-002 — P1/P2 correctness**

I would classify it P1 if brand-specific content is legally/business materially different; otherwise P2.

This should be resolved before declaring the V2 delivery contract authoritative.

---

# SU-TUTORIAL-V2-003 — Repository comments no longer match schema identity

There are several comments saying:

```text
ONE tutorial per subtopic per brand
```

and:

```text
Identity: (subtopicId, brandId)
```

But the actual current schema has evolved to:

```text
subtopicId
+
navigationNodeId
+
brandId
```

The database's active unique index correctly reflects the newer identity.

So executable schema is ahead of some repository/service documentation.

This doesn't break production directly, but stale architectural comments are dangerous here because this is a core domain identity.

**Disposition: P2 documentation/code coherence cleanup.**

---

# SU-TUTORIAL-V2-004 — Excessive diagnostic logging remains inside repository writes

`TutorialSectionRepository.createTutorial()` constructs a diagnostic identifier using `Date.now()` and emits multiple `console.log()` statements covering:

```text
subtopic
brand
order
status
version
block count
```

On failure it logs:

```text
database error type
message
code
detail
constraint
table
column
stack
```

That is useful during development but too much low-level persistence diagnostic information for normal production repository behavior.

The repository should normally throw a typed error and let controlled observability capture appropriate details.

### Classification

**P2 — observability / SRP concern**

Not security-critical by itself, but worth cleaning as part of production hardening.

---

# SU-TUTORIAL-V2-005 — `any` weakens an otherwise strongly typed repository

The new repository repeatedly uses patterns like:

```ts
brandId as any
```

and:

```ts
const updateData: any = ...
```

That weakens precisely the part of the architecture where explicit contracts are valuable.

Examples include:

```text
brand identity
status transitions
TutorialDocument persistence
update structures
```

The architecture should derive these types from the Drizzle schema or explicit domain types.

I would not create a hierarchy of interfaces purely for SOLID; simply removing unnecessary `any` would give us more value with less complexity.

**Classification: P2 — type-safety weakness.**

---

# New architecture vs legacy architecture

We can now make a much stronger architectural decision.

| Concern | Legacy `tutorial_content` | V2 `tutorial_sections` |
|---|---|---|
| Brand stored in record | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Brand visibility contract | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Navigation-page identity | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Soft deletion | ✅ | ✅ |
| Publication lifecycle | Simple boolean | Explicit statuses |
| Learner-safe sanitization | ❌ Not demonstrated | ✅ Present |
| Content schema validation on delivery | Weak/legacy cast | ✅ `TutorialDocumentSchema` |
| Brand filtering during query | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Supports current ILS model | Legacy | Designed for it |
| Architecture direction | Retire | Preserve/evolve |

My Principal Architect recommendation therefore changes from:

> “Implement brand filtering in the legacy engine.”

to:

> **Do not invest heavily in making the legacy `tutorial_content` engine a second correct brand-aware content architecture unless active callers require a transitional fix. The correct long-term authority should be `tutorial_sections` + `TutorialDeliveryService`.**

That respects KISS, YAGNI and single ownership.

# Progress architecture review expanded

I also reviewed the legacy `TutorialProgressRepository`.

It has a database unique index on:

```text
(userId, subtopicId)
```

which is positive.

But `markBlockComplete()` follows:

```text
read existing row
        ↓
compute merged blocks in application memory
        ↓
update row
```

This is not equivalent to the newer ILS atomic SQL model.

Two concurrent completion requests can potentially read the same old `blocksCompleted` value and write competing updates.

The `version` field is incremented:

```text
version = version + 1
```

but the update does **not compare an expected version**.

Therefore the version counter is not optimistic concurrency control.

### SU-PROGRESS-005 — P1/P2 — Legacy progress can lose concurrent completions

Conceptually:

```text
existing = [notes]

Request A reads [notes]
Request B reads [notes]

A adds code
→ [notes, code]

B adds technical
→ [notes, technical]
```

Depending on ordering, one update can overwrite the other.

The newer ILS database helpers previously reviewed use much stronger atomic database expressions.

This is another reason to avoid maintaining two authoritative progress systems.

---

# Interaction routes: secure scoring improved, progress architecture still broken

I also re-reviewed the current quiz/practice/completion interaction path.

There is an important positive:

## SU-INTERACTION-001 — Positive — Quiz and practice answers are server-authoritative

Both quiz and practice now derive the answer from stored tutorial section content using:

```text
extractCorrectAnswerFromContent(section.content, questionId)
```

If an authoritative answer cannot be found:

```http
422
```

is returned.

Client-provided `correctAnswer` is no longer scoring authority.

That remediation should be preserved.

---

# But the comments are stale

The quiz header comment still describes an older strategy involving:

```text
previous correct answer
or client fallback on first attempt
```

while the executable implementation correctly does neither.

Practice has similar stale commentary.

### SU-CODE-DOC-001 — P2

Security comments contradict the current secure implementation.

This matters because future maintainers could “fix” the code back toward the obsolete behavior after reading misleading comments.

**Disposition: update comments during remediation, without changing current scoring authority.**

---

# SU-INTERACTION-002 remains confirmed — returned progress is fake/placeholder

The shared helper:

```ts
updateProgressForSection(...)
```

does not inspect actual progress.

It returns:

```text
calculateTutorialProgress({
    completedSections: []
})
```

Every caller therefore receives progress equivalent to an empty completion state.

So after a learner successfully answers a quiz or finishes an interaction:

```text
database interaction record
        ✅ real
progress returned in same response
        ❌ placeholder
```

This is not merely technical debt if frontend code consumes that response.

### Classification

**P1 if active UI relies on it.**

The correct solution is not to add more logic here.

The interaction API should use the canonical ILS progress application service, or stop returning misleading progress altogether during migration.

---

# SU-INTERACTION-004 — Attempt numbering race remains

Quiz and practice calculate:

```text
existing attempts
        ↓
length + 1
        ↓
insert
```

That is a standard concurrency race.

Two simultaneous submissions can both calculate:

```text
attemptNumber = 3
```

unless a database constraint prevents it.

I attempted to inspect the corresponding schema paths, but those schema filenames are not at the conventional paths I tried, so I am **not yet claiming database constraints are absent**.

Current status:

**Code-level race confirmed. Database-level protection still unverified.**

---

# SU-INTERACTION-005 — Quiz score meaning is problematic

The GET endpoint computes:

```ts
correctAnswers / totalAttempts * 100
```

while reporting:

```text
totalQuestions = count(distinct questionIds attempted)
```

Those represent different denominators/concepts.

A learner who attempts one question ten times and succeeds once receives:

```text
totalQuestions: 1
totalAttempts: 10
correctAnswers: 1
score: 10
```

That may be useful as an **attempt accuracy rate**.

It is not necessarily a quiz score.

### Recommendation

Define these separately:

```text
question completion
latest-answer correctness
first-attempt correctness
attempt accuracy
assessment score
```

Do not overload them into one ambiguous `score`.

**Classification: P1/P2 business-contract issue depending on downstream use.**

---

# SU-INTERACTION-007 — Correct answers are written to logs

When the browser submits a mismatched `correctAnswer`, quiz/practice currently log both:

```text
clientValue
authoritativeValue
```

The server should certainly detect tampering.

But logging the authoritative answer key is unnecessary.

For an education/assessment system, answer keys are sensitive application data.

Log instead:

```text
questionId
mismatch = true
request/correlation ID
possibly learner identifier hash
```

not the correct answer.

**Classification: P2 assessment confidentiality.**

---

# SkillUp-web Principal Architect Audit — Expanded Review, Round 1 of 6

Repository: `skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC`\
Branch: `feature/project-llm-linux-worker`\
Scope: `apps/skillup-web`, its shared UI modules, authentication boundaries, backend APIs and database dependencies.

This round continues the existing audit rather than restarting it. The review remains read-only, and the 5–6-round target is a planning objective, not a reason to certify files that have not been inspected.

## New confirmed finding: server-side API helper forwards untrusted identity headers

SU-IDENTITY-004 · P1 investigation priority

In [src/lib/skillup-api.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/lib/skillup-api.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com), `fetchSkillupApi()` reads `x-shadow-user-id`, `x-original-user-id`, `x-portal-identity` and `x-brand` from incoming Next.js request headers, then forwards them to an absolute application URL.

It also forwards the request cookie and adds `GATEWAY_TRUST_SECRET` when configured.

The concern is provenance: these values must originate from a validated authentication boundary, not merely from headers that happen to be present. This is especially important because the outgoing request can carry a service-trust credential alongside them.

This is not yet a demonstrated impersonation vulnerability. It requires an end-to-end check of the middleware's header sanitization, deployment routing and downstream verification before assigning exploitability.

The helper does correctly use `cache: 'no-store'` and avoids protected learner-data fallbacks when a protected API request fails. Those protections should be preserved.

## New confirmed finding: attendance percentage uses a questionable denominator

SU-ATTENDANCE-001 · P2 data-contract issue

The actual [student attendance page](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/student/attendance/page.tsx?utm_source=chatgpt.com) computes:

```
presentDays / history.length * 100
```

The same page counts late arrivals separately. Consequently, a late arrival counts in the denominator but not the numerator, and the metric's label does not explain that policy.

This may be correct if the academy defines attendance strictly as on-time presence. If late arrival should count toward attendance, the displayed percentage is understated.

The authoritative attendance policy should live in the learner domain; the React page should display the agreed metric rather than invent a competing business definition.

## New confirmed finding: dashboard contains excessive server-side authentication logging

SU-LOG-002 · P2 observability hygiene

The [dashboard page](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/dashboard/page.tsx?utm_source=chatgpt.com) logs authentication decisions, truncated identity, roles, onboarding state and redirect decisions during server rendering.

Authentication diagnostics are useful, but ordinary dashboard rendering should not produce identity-linked console logs on every request. Structured, sampled and appropriately redacted authentication events would be more suitable.

The page positively enforces an authentication check and redirects unauthenticated users before invoking `resolveDashboardData()`. That ordering is worth retaining.

## Round 1 continued — findings from the expanded file review

The additional inspection now covers the student workspace, public catalogue, faculty pages, shared API helper, UI components, configuration, authentication routes and ILS BFF routes.

## Open

The 58 files are successfully retrieved source files in this round, including some previously examined files revisited for cross-file tracing. Missing paths are excluded. This is not a claim that all 137 tracked application files have been audited.

### Additional findings requiring attention

| ID              | Priority | Confirmed issue                                                                                                                                   |
| --------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| SU-UI-001       | P2       | Student dashboard KPI progress bars use fixed visual widths of 86%, 68%, 54% and 62%, rather than the actual metric values                        |
| SU-UI-002       | P2       | Payments page contains nonfunctional Pay overdue installment and Download receipt buttons                                                         |
| SU-UI-003       | P2       | Exams page shows hardcoded exam availability and nonfunctional Start practice buttons                                                             |
| SU-LEARN-001    | P1/P2    | `/student/learn` presents a hardcoded three-module learning path rather than actual enrolled tutorial content                                     |
| SU-FACULTY-001  | P2       | Faculty page maps backend statistics to icons by array position, creating fragile presentation coupling                                           |
| SU-PROGRAMS-001 | P1/P2    | Public-facing programme pages use APIs requiring authentication, creating inconsistent public-catalogue behavior                                  |
| SU-API-002      | P2       | Catalogue API failures trigger direct database fallback, mixing transport and persistence responsibilities                                        |
| SU-UI-004       | P2       | Session calendar moves focus programmatically and supports keyboard navigation, but the empty-session and changing-session behavior needs testing |
| SU-CONFIG-002   | P2       | TypeScript excludes test files, so the normal application type-check cannot detect inconsistencies inside tests                                   |
| SU-TEST-002     | P1       | Existing proxy test imports an export absent from the reviewed proxy implementation and assumes an unauthenticated RSC bypass                     |
| SU-ILS-013      | P2       | ILS proxy routes duplicate URL, credential, error-handling and response logic                                                                     |
| SU-ILS-014      | P2       | The ILS visit route retains production `console.log` diagnostics containing upstream routing information                                          |

### Three important architectural observations

1\. The real learner UI is not yet wired to the tutorial domain.

The [SkillUp learn page](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/student/learn/page.tsx?utm_source=chatgpt.com) contains a static array of React, Next.js and API-integration modules.

The [exams page](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/student/exams/page.tsx?utm_source=chatgpt.com) similarly contains static assessment tracks and action buttons without handlers.

This is a consequential answer to our earlier caller-tracing question: these two active student pages do not themselves consume the legacy tutorial-content API or the new ILS delivery API. It does not prove no other frontend component consumes them.

Before declaring the learning architecture ready, the actual learner navigation must be connected to authoritative enrolment, tutorial delivery and assessment records—or the pages must be explicitly identified as demonstrations rather than operational learner experiences.

2\. Public catalogue authentication is inconsistent.

The [programmes page](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/programs/page.tsx?utm_source=chatgpt.com) is written as a public discovery experience, and the proxy test expects public catalogue accessibility. However, [the programmes API](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/api/programs/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) requires authenticated, brand-validated identity.

The shared `fetchSkillupApi()` then falls back to direct data helpers when public programme requests fail.

That may keep server-rendered catalogue pages working, but it makes the two execution paths behave differently and obscures which layer authorizes catalogue access.

Recommended decision: Define the public programme-read contract explicitly. Public catalogue data should not require an authenticated learner identity unless the product requires it.

3\. The application contains user-visible actions that do not work.

The [payments page](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/student/payments/page.tsx?utm_source=chatgpt.com) renders two real-looking action buttons, neither with a click handler, form submission or navigation.

The exams page does the same for practice initiation.

This is a product correctness issue, not just an aesthetic concern. In a financial interface, an action that looks operational but does nothing can mislead learners.

The remediation should be either a real authorized workflow or an explicit unavailable state—not a button with no behavior.

### Positive code decisions to preserve

The review also identified several good implementations:

- `SiteShell` separates global layout from route-specific chrome.
- Student API routes use `requireStudentAuth()` before returning learner data.
- Student server-rendered pages use a common `fetchSkillupApi()` helper.
- Protected learner data requests do not fall back to fabricated responses inside that helper.
- `SessionCalendar` includes tab roles, arrow-key handling, Home/End navigation and visible focus styles.
- The auth login/signup pages reuse shared authentication UI rather than implementing a duplicate authentication system.
- The session-management BFF routes delegate to shared authentication services.
- The isolated test-session route has negative tests for production deployment flags and invalid fixture secrets.
- The ILS BFF routes consistently authenticate before forwarding tracking events.

These are important because the eventual remediation should be targeted, rather than a wholesale rewrite.

Reviewed this round

Complete actual frontend caller inventory, shared branding components, onboarding, dashboard resolver, authentication middleware and identity propagation.

Round 6 — Consolidation and architecture decision

Reconcile all findings, identify gaps against the full file inventory, rank remediation, define tests, and prepare the implementation approval package.

Principal Architect decision: Continue the read-only baseline. The code now demonstrates a mix of production-grade authentication boundaries and unfinished or placeholder learner experiences. The architecture should not be accepted until those gaps, the actual tutorial callers and database ownership contracts are reconciled.

# SkillUp-web — Principal Architect Audit, 18-File Review

Repository: `skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC`\
Authoritative branch: `feature/project-llm-linux-worker`\
Application: `apps/skillup-web`\
Review type: Read-only, statement-level source inspection, security and architectural review.

I have reviewed 18 source files in this tranche, concentrating on authentication, tutorial content delivery, interaction tracking, progress, and test coverage. Some files were previously inspected; this pass revisits them together to trace behavior across boundaries.

The central finding is that SkillUp has sound authentication delegation in several places, but its tutorial APIs do not consistently implement the same identity, validation, caching, and upstream-routing contracts.

## 2. Most significant findings

### SU-AUTH-006 — P1: Logout cookie-scope mismatch

The SkillUp logout BFF invokes the central auth service and then reconstructs cookie deletion locally:

```
response.cookies.set(name, '', {
  httpOnly: true,
  secure: true,
  sameSite: 'none',
  maxAge: 0,
  path: '/',
});
```

It omits the original cookie's `domain` attribute.

The previous cross-file review found that shared authentication issues SkillUp cookies with a domain-scoped policy.

Deleting a host-only cookie is not necessarily equivalent to deleting the domain-scoped cookie originally issued.

Impact: Session clearing may behave inconsistently across hosts or browser states.

Recommended design: Preserve the authoritative `Set-Cookie` deletion contract from the shared authentication service or use a shared cookie-policy implementation. Test exact domain, path and SameSite behavior.

### SU-TUTORIAL-008 — P1: Inconsistent upstream-routing contracts

The tutorial routes use several slightly different upstream paths.

| SkillUp endpoint      | Constructed upstream path                 |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| General progress      | `/api/tutorial/progress`                  |
| ILS subtopic progress | `/api/tutorial/ils/subtopic/.../progress` |
| ILS visit             | `/tutorial/ils/visit`                     |
| Tutorial sections     | `/tutorial/sections/...`                  |
| Legacy content        | `/api/tutorial/content/...`               |
| Interactions          | `/tutorial/interactions/...`              |

Some environments may deliberately rewrite paths, so this alone does not prove they fail in production.

However, the application lacks one visibly authoritative routing contract. Individual handlers independently build service URLs and credentials.

Architectural impact: DRY, consistency, testability and gateway boundary ownership.

Recommended design: One small, typed internal API client that owns base URL normalization, service credentials, timeouts, error mapping and route conventions.

### SU-CACHE-002 — P1/P2: Personalized progress responses use `no-cache`

The progress handlers return:

```
Cache-Control: no-cache
```

This permits storage subject to revalidation. It is not equivalent to preventing storage.

Because progress contains learner-specific data, the safer contract is normally:

```
Cache-Control: private, no-store
```

This matters particularly in this application because the service worker's caching policy was already identified as a privacy-review priority.

The sections BFF correctly uses `private, no-store`; the progress BFF does not. This inconsistency is confirmed.

### SU-ILS-015 — P2: BFF input validation is uneven

The general tutorial-progress route uses Zod schemas to validate UUIDs, section types and the literal status `viewed`.

By contrast, the ILS subtopic progress route interpolates the incoming `subtopicId` directly into an upstream URL:

```
const url = `${apiUrl}/api/tutorial/ils/subtopic/${params.subtopicId}/progress`;
```

The sections route likewise forwards an unvalidated path parameter and copies arbitrary query parameters upstream.

The backend may reject invalid inputs, so these are defense-in-depth and contract-consistency issues rather than confirmed database corruption.

Recommended design: Validate identifiers with canonical request schemas and explicitly define allowed query parameters at the BFF boundary.

### SU-INTERACTION-008 — P2: Interaction proxy forwards unparsed request bodies

The interaction route correctly restricts interaction types to:

`quiz`, `practice`, `code`, `visual`, `completion`.

That is positive.

However, POST forwards:

```
body: await request.text()
```

and forwards the caller's content type.

The BFF performs no body-schema validation; it relies on the upstream API. Previous backend review found stronger schema validation there, which reduces risk.

I would preserve backend authority and add BFF validation only if it meaningfully improves the public API contract, not duplicate an entire business validator.

### SU-ILS-016 — P1 investigation: Learning-session identifier provenance

The ILS visit and block-visit routes forward the browser's:

```
x-session-id
```

directly to the backend, while learner identity is server-derived.

The browser may legitimately select an active learning session, but its session identifier cannot itself constitute proof of ownership.

The backend must establish:

```
Authenticated learner
    ↓
Authorized session membership
    ↓
Allowed activity write
```

Whether that happens completely in the progress service and repository remains the important verification point.

## 3. Authentication design: good separation, but contracts need consolidation

Signup, password recovery, verification, login and refresh are appropriately thin wrappers around `proxyAuthRequest()`.

This is desirable. SkillUp should not duplicate:

- password hashing,
- token signing,
- refresh-token rotation,
- identity creation,
- session revocation.

The shared authority should implement those rules once.

The exception is logout, where the SkillUp BFF reconstructs cookie-clearing semantics instead of simply preserving the complete shared contract.

The test-fixture endpoint also demonstrates substantial security care: long secret, timing-safe comparison, tenant/fixture allowlists, UUID validation and short-lived tokens. But the `PROJECT_LLM_ISOLATED_VERIFICATION` override means `NODE_ENV=production` alone does not disable token issuance. Deployment isolation must therefore be an enforceable security invariant, not just a convention.

## 4. Engineering principles assessment

| Principle              | Assessment for these 18 files                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Single Responsibility  | Mostly strong for auth wrappers; weaker in tutorial handlers that combine auth, input processing, routing and error translation |
| Open/Closed            | Interaction type allowlist is explicit; new interaction types require coordinated backend changes                               |
| Liskov Substitution    | No relevant polymorphic hierarchy found in this tranche                                                                         |
| Interface Segregation  | Not sufficiently applicable to these route files alone                                                                          |
| Dependency Inversion   | Auth wrappers delegate correctly; tutorial BFF depends directly on environment-specific upstream details                        |
| DRY                    | Confirmed duplication in tutorial BFF                                                                                           |
| KISS                   | Thin authentication routes are a good example; repeated hand-built upstream requests are not                                    |
| YAGNI                  | Do not introduce a large generic proxy framework; a focused internal client is sufficient                                       |
| Separation of Concerns | Content authoring is correctly blocked from the learner application                                                             |
| Security by Default    | Partial: authentication is consistently invoked, but cache, session identity and service credential handling need alignment     |
| Testability            | Some targeted tests exist; important regression scenarios remain uncovered                                                      |

## 5. Required verification before accepting these findings as resolved

The eventual test suite should establish that an unauthenticated learner cannot reach protected tutorial APIs; that cross-brand identity and missing shadow identities are rejected as specified; that personal progress responses cannot enter shared caches; that original cookies are cleared during logout; that session IDs cannot write to other learners' records; and that malformed content and interaction identifiers produce consistent errors.

The current progress tests verify upstream URL normalization and authentication forwarding. They do not establish the whole behavior above.

## Principal Architect conclusion

This tranche reinforces three architectural decisions.

First, preserve shared authentication ownership. Do not copy authentication logic into SkillUp.

Second, standardize tutorial BFF contracts. The current independent fetch implementations have accumulated inconsistent URL paths, validation rules, cache policies, session headers and error responses.

Third, consolidate learning progress under the newer ILS domain rather than extending the legacy progress and interaction systems into permanent parallel authorities.

The next review should prioritize 15–20 not-yet-reviewed backend and shared UI dependency files, especially the full `LearningProgressService`, navigation progress repositories, real learner-content consumers and interaction schema constraints. That will provide the evidence needed to close the pending questions rather than simply repeat the identified risks.

Audit status: In progress. Phase 2A/2B not accepted. Zero modifications.

# SkillUp-web Principal Architect Audit — 20–30 File Tranche

Repository: `skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC`\
Branch: `feature/project-llm-linux-worker`\
Reference architecture: `FinalAechitecture.md`\
Mode: Read-only source review; no code changes or test execution.

This tranche focuses on a critical architectural question: does the learner application derive identity, permissions and learner data from one trusted authority, or do separate code paths apply conflicting rules?

## Confirmed finding 1 — Authentication middleware has a fail-open gateway-secret condition

SU-AUTH-007 · P1

File: [src/share-branding/middleware/authProxy.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/src/share-branding/middleware/authProxy.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The `hasValidGatewaySecret()` helper returns `true` when `INTERNAL_GATEWAY_SECRET` is missing or empty:

```
if (
  typeof INTERNAL_GATEWAY_SECRET !== 'string' ||
  INTERNAL_GATEWAY_SECRET.length === 0
) {
  return true;
}
```

That is a confirmed fail-open condition in the gateway-secret check.

Security qualification: It does not automatically prove an unauthorized user can access learner data, because JWT verification and authorization checks also exist. But it removes a defense that the surrounding code appears to treat as a security requirement.

The architecture calls for explicit server-side identity, tenant validation and protected internal service boundaries. Missing trust configuration should not silently count as a valid gateway secret where that secret is required.

## Confirmed finding 2 — Authentication implementations disagree about learner identity

SU-IDENTITY-005 · P1

Two shared authentication paths return different identity semantics.

In `apps/skillup-web/src/lib/student-auth.ts`, the student BFF prefers:

```
payload.shadowUserId ?? payload.userId
```

In `src/share-branding/auth/unifiedBffAuth.ts`, `createInternalHeaders()` instead sets:

```
'x-user-id': auth.originalUserId
```

The middleware sets `x-user-id` to the shadow user ID.

These may represent legitimately different domains, but the distinction is not expressed in the downstream API contracts. A consumer of `x-user-id` cannot safely infer whether it contains a global person ID or a SkillUp-local learner ID without knowing which producer forwarded it.

Required architectural decision: Keep both identifiers where necessary, but define one explicit contract per receiving service. Never overload an ambiguously named identity header across database boundaries.

## Confirmed finding 3 — Learner data helper still contains fictional operational data

SU-DATA-006 · P1

File: [apps/skillup-web/src/lib/skillup-data.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/lib/skillup-data.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The module contains hardcoded programmes, faculty, batch sessions, placement profiles and job matches.

More importantly, some production-facing functions return those values when real data is missing or an upstream database operation fails.

Examples confirmed by inspection:

- `getSkillupPrograms()` returns fallback programmes for empty results or exceptions.
- `getSkillupBatches()` returns a fabricated batch when the learner has no active batch.
- `getSkillupFaculty()` returns invented faculty information on database failure.
- `getSkillupPlacement()` returns a default readiness profile when no active placement profile exists.

This violates the expected distinction between real learner data, an empty state, and a failed dependency.

It is especially concerning for financial, attendance and placement-related user experiences, where users should not mistake demonstration values for authoritative records.

## Confirmed finding 4 — Shared identity documentation contradicts active consumers

SU-IDENTITY-006 · P1

The [identity guard](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/src/share-branding/auth/identityGuard.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) explicitly declares:

- `originalUserId` is for brand-specific database operations.
- `shadowUserId` is for cross-brand observability.
- `getDatabaseUserId()` deliberately rejects a missing `originalUserId`.

Yet `requireStudentAuth()` returns the shadow ID as its primary `userId`, and the student API routes pass that ID to database queries.

This is a confirmed contract contradiction, not proof that every query uses the wrong record. That depends on actual database keys.

Remediation: Establish a canonical identity model with distinct types such as `GlobalPersonId` and `BrandLearnerId`, then verify each repository's foreign keys against that model.

## Confirmed finding 5 — Dashboard displays synthetic progress as learner achievements

SU-DASH-004 · P1/P2

The [dashboard data builder](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/src/share-branding/dashboardPageData.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) derives mastery scores from the learner's declared skill level:

```
beginner: [42, 58, 64],
intermediate: [68, 76, 88],
advanced: [90, 94, 79],
```

It also constructs simulated activity events, a streak value, recommendations and progress milestones based on onboarding state.

These are not measured learner achievements.

Recommendation: Keep onboarding preferences separate from assessed skill mastery and historical activity. If the current view is illustrative, label the data as illustrative rather than presenting it as measured performance.

## Confirmed finding 6 — Service worker caches authenticated navigations

SU-CACHE-001 · P1 · Reconfirmed

The [SkillUp service worker](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/sw.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) caches any successful same-origin navigation response without checking its privacy headers.

This includes the possibility of caching authenticated learner HTML.

Consequences could include stale progress after updates or account-specific content surviving logout on a shared browser.

The architecture requires public assets to be cacheable while authenticated responses remain private.

Required change: Separate public asset caching from personalized navigation policies and test logout, offline access and account switching.

## Confirmed finding 7 — Shared auth-forwarding helper preserves caller-supplied sensitive headers

SU-AUTH-008 · P1 investigation

In [authBffRoute.ts](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/src/share-branding/auth/authBffRoute.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com), `createForwardHeaders()` begins with a copy of the incoming request headers.

It removes some transport headers and overwrites selected brand and secret headers. However, it does not clearly establish a full denylist for caller-supplied identity headers such as `x-user-id`, `x-shadow-user-id` or `x-original-user-id`.

Risk: Downstream trust becomes dependent on whether the gateway rejects or replaces these headers.

This requires an integration test with forged incoming identity headers to establish actual exploitability.

## Confirmed finding 8 — Host-based URL construction is inconsistent

SU-AUTH-009 · P2

`validateAuthState.ts` intentionally avoids trusting `x-forwarded-host` for brand resolution.

Conversely, `serverAuthState.ts` constructs its target URL using `x-forwarded-host` before `host`.

`placement-handoff/route.ts` also prefers `x-forwarded-host` when rewriting refreshed cookies.

These different policies are a significant source of ambiguity in a shared gateway architecture.

Recommendation: Define one trusted request-origin contract, including which infrastructure components may set forwarded headers.

## Confirmed finding 9 — Onboarding routing differs from shared gateway configuration

SU-ONBOARD-003 · P2

The [SkillUp onboarding API](https://github.com/skillupitacademy-alt/SUIA_RTH_SHC/blob/feature/project-llm-linux-worker/apps/skillup-web/src/app/api/onboarding/route.ts?utm_source=chatgpt.com) selects `GATEWAY_URL_SKILLUP` for SkillUp hosts, while the shared auth proxy uses `GATEWAY_URL`.

It also forwards the request body without a local schema-validation step.

The gateway URLs may resolve to the same service in deployment. That configuration equivalence remains unverified.

The architecture should not require route authors to make independent decisions about gateway origins.

## Confirmed finding 10 — Auth-validation timeout cleanup is not guaranteed

SU-AUTH-010 · P2

`validateAuthState.ts` and `serverAuthState.ts` create abort timers inside retry loops and clear them on some successful paths.

Several early returns and exception paths lack guaranteed cleanup.

A `try/finally` around each timed request would make the behavior predictable and reduce unnecessary retained timers during request failures.

### Principal Architect assessment

The highest-priority remediation themes are now clear:

1. Identity integrity: Resolve `originalUserId` versus `shadowUserId` before relying on learner database operations.
2. Security boundaries: Require correctly configured trust secrets; sanitize identity headers before trusted upstream calls.
3. Data correctness: Remove fabricated progress, attendance, placement and batch information from operational learner experiences.
4. Caching: Never persist personalized learner responses in a shared or offline cache without an explicit privacy-safe design.
5. Routing consistency: Centralize gateway and request-origin decisions.

The source confirms these inconsistencies, but it does not establish that the corresponding production vulnerabilities have been exploited. Runtime testing, database-key verification and deployment configuration review remain necessary.

Current result: 25 files retrieved and audited at the source level, with major functions and call relationships inspected. Long shared modules still warrant targeted tests and further dependency tracing before an exhaustive line-by-line certification.

Repository changes: 0. Tests executed: 0. Audit acceptance: Pending.
